question: - A source, published sometime between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2018, explains the variation of difficulty depending on the target in a certain activity. In this source, the third word in the first paragraph is "game." You are a research assistant. Your only tool is `web_search` (up to 10 searches).
After each search, the most promising results are opened automatically, their links
are followed, and notes from the most relevant pages come back with the results.
Your job is to write the queries that reach the right pages.

Each query targets one page that would state or link to a missing fact: an entity's
profile, a discography or list, an official record, an interview, an article.
Do not put the whole question into one query.
- Use enough words to preserve the identifying relation. Combine two or three
  distinctive conditions when helpful; there is no fixed word-count limit.
  Quote exact names or titles, not generic descriptions.
- Distinguish question-given constraints, source-supported facts and guesses.
  Do not turn a guessed country, nationality, date or identity into a required
  query filter. Search the stated relation before assuming its answer values.
  If a hypothesis-specific query finds no support, remove that assumed filter
  and return to the question's constraints rather than cycling through guesses.
- Once a candidate appears, search the candidate's name with the condition still
  unverified (e.g. `<name> interview 2013`, `<name> discography label`).
- Reuse exact names, titles and terms from the notes; they are better query words
  than paraphrases of the question.
- Review candidates in the returned notes before every search. Keep new candidates
  pending until investigated or explicitly excluded by source evidence. Prefer
  checking a distinctive missing condition of a source-backed candidate before
  returning to an unsupported guess. If you defer a candidate, explain why.
- Never repeat or lightly reword an earlier query. If a query returned nothing
  useful, switch to a different clue or a different kind of source, not a synonym.

Before each search, write in your reasoning: the current candidate(s), which
conditions are confirmed, contradicted or unknown, and what the next query should
find.

Notes are free-form readings of individual pages. Treat reported source facts
as evidence and tentative candidates as leads to verify. A mention alone does
not establish all conditions. Compare candidates against every
condition, revise on explicit contradictions, and preserve unknowns as unknowns.
When evidence supports an answer, give it in the requested format with source URLs.
Never invent missing facts or treat a JEV ranking score as answer confidence.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Using a bow to shoot arrows

For other uses, see [Archery (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery_(disambiguation) "Archery (disambiguation)").

"Archer" redirects here. For other uses, see [Archer (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archer_(disambiguation) "Archer (disambiguation)").

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/ArcheryGermanyEarly1980s-2.jpg/330px-ArcheryGermanyEarly1980s-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ArcheryGermanyEarly1980s-2.jpg)

Archery competition in June 1983 at [Mönchengladbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6nchengladbach "Mönchengladbach"), [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany")

**Archery** is the sport, practice, or skill of using a [bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_and_arrow "Bow and arrow") to [shoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shooting "Shooting")[arrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow "Arrow") at a target.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-Paterson17-1) The word comes from the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin")_arcus_, meaning bow.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-2) Historically, archery has been used for hunting and combat. In modern times, it is mainly a competitive sport and recreational activity. A person who practices archery is typically called an **archer**, **bowman**, or **toxophilite**.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_archery "History of archery")

### Origins and ancient archery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origins and ancient archery")]

The oldest known evidence of [arrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow "Arrow") (not found with surviving bows) comes from [South African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") sites such as [Sibudu Cave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sibudu_Cave "Sibudu Cave"), where the remains of bone and stone arrowheads have been found dating approximately 72,000 to 60,000 years ago.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-Lombard2020-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-Backwell-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-Lombard-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-Lombard_M-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-Backwell2018-9)

However, the earliest remains of complete bows and arrows are found in [Northern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Europe "Northern Europe"). These include the evidence found at Mannheim-Vogelstang, in modern-day [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), dated 17,500 to 18,000 years ago, and also at Stellmoor dated 11,000 years ago.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-10)

[Azilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azilian "Azilian") points found in [Grotte du Bichon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grotte_du_Bichon "Grotte du Bichon"), Switzerland, alongside the remains of both a bear and a hunter, with flint fragments found in the bear's third vertebra, suggest the use of arrows at 13,500 years ago.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-11)

Other signs of its use in Europe come from the [Stellmoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellmoor?action=edit&redlink=1 "Stellmoor (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellmoor "de:Stellmoor")] in the [Ahrensburg valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahrensburg_valley?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ahrensburg valley (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellmoor%E2%80%93Ahrensburger%20Tunneltal "de:Stellmoor–Ahrensburger Tunneltal")] north of [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"), Germany and dates from the late [Paleolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleolithic "Paleolithic"), about 10,000–9000 BC. The arrows were made of [pine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pine "Pine") and consisted of a main shaft and a 15–20 cm (5.9–7.9 in) fore shaft with a [flint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flint "Flint") point. There are no definite earlier bows; previous pointed shafts are known, but may have been launched by [spear-throwers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spear-thrower "Spear-thrower") rather than bows. The [oldest bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holmegaard_bow "Holmegaard bow") known so far comes from the [Holmegård](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holmegaard "Holmegaard") swamp in Denmark. At the site of [Nataruk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nataruk "Nataruk") in [Turkana County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkana_County "Turkana County"), Kenya, [obsidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obsidian "Obsidian") bladelets found embedded in a skull and within the thoracic cavity of another skeleton, suggest the use of stone-tipped arrows as weapons about 10,000 years ago.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-12) Bows eventually replaced the [spear-thrower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spear-thrower "Spear-thrower") as the predominant means for launching shafted [projectiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projectiles "Projectiles"), on every continent except [Australasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australasia "Australasia"), though spear-throwers persisted alongside the bow in parts of the Americas, including Mexico and among the [Inuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inuit "Inuit").

Bows and arrows have been present in [Egyptian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") and neighbouring [Nubian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubia "Nubia") culture since its respective [predynastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predynastic_Egypt "Predynastic Egypt") and [Pre-Kerma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Kerma "Pre-Kerma") origins. In the [Levant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levant "Levant"), artifacts that could be arrow-shaft straighteners are known from the [Natufian culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natufian_culture "Natufian culture"), (c. 10,800–8,300 BC) onwards.

[Classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_antiquity "Classical antiquity") civilizations, notably the [Babylonians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylonia "Babylonia"), [Assyrians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Assyrians "Ancient Assyrians"), [Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece"), [Armenians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Armenia "History of Armenia"), [Persians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire"), [Parthians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthia "Parthia"), [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"), [Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_India "History of India"), [Koreans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Korea "History of Korea"), [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_China "History of China"), and [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Japan "History of Japan") fielded large numbers of archers in their armies. [Akkadians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akkadian_Empire "Akkadian Empire") were the first to use [composite bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_bows "Composite bows") in war according to the victory stele of [Naram-Sin of Akkad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naram-Sin_of_Akkad "Naram-Sin of Akkad").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-13) Egyptians referred to [Nubia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubia "Nubia") as "Ta-Seti," or "The Land of the Bow," since the Nubians were known to be expert archers, and by the 16th century BC Egyptians were using the composite bow in warfare.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-14) The Bronze Age Aegean Cultures were able to deploy a number of state-owned specialized bow makers for warfare and hunting purposes already from the 15th century BC.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-15) The [Welsh longbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_longbow "Welsh longbow") proved its worth for the first time in Continental warfare at the [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-16) In the Americas archery was widespread at European contact.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-17)

Archery was highly developed in Asia. The composite bow was likely invented in [central Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asia "Central Asia"), with the [Scythians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scythians "Scythians") being the likely inventors of the first composite bows.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-Loades-18) The [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") term for archery, [dhanurvidya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhanurveda "Dhanurveda"), came to refer to martial arts in general. In East Asia, [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo"), one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea was well known for its regiments of exceptionally skilled archers.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-koreantrad-20)

### Medieval archery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Medieval archery")]

The medieval shortbow was technically identical with the classical era bows, having a range of approximately 91 m (299 ft). It was the primary ranged weapon of the battlefield through the early medieval period. Around the tenth century the [crossbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossbow "Crossbow") was introduced in Europe. Crossbows generally had a longer range, greater accuracy and more penetration than the shortbow, but suffered from a much slower rate of fire. Crossbows were used in the early [Crusades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades "Crusades"), with models having a range of 274 m (899 ft) and being able to penetrate armour or kill a horse.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-21)

During the late medieval period the English army famously relied on massed archers armed with the [longbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbow "Longbow"). The French army relied more on the crossbow.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-22) Like their predecessors archers were more likely to be peasants or yeomen than men-at-arms. The longbow had a range of up to 270 m (890 ft). However its lack of accuracy at long ranges made it a mass weapon rather than an individual one. Significant victories attributable to the longbow, such as the [Battle of Crecy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Crecy "Battle of Crecy")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-23) and [Battle of Agincourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt "Battle of Agincourt") resulted in the [English longbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow "English longbow") becoming part of military lore.

### Mounted archery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mounted archery")]

Main article: [Mounted archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mounted_archery "Mounted archery")

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Maximilian_1470.png/250px-Maximilian_1470.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Maximilian_1470.png)

Hunting for flying birds from the back of a galloping horse was considered the top category of archery. The favourite hobby of Prince [Maximilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor"), engraved by [Dürer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCrer "Dürer")

The [Scythians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scythians "Scythians") became extremely adept at [archery on horseback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mounted_archery "Mounted archery"), and may have invented the first true composite bow, which they spread across Europe and Asia.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-Loades-18) Lightly armoured, but highly mobile archers were excellently suited to warfare in the Central Asian steppes, and they formed a large part of armies that repeatedly conquered large areas of Eurasia. Shorter bows are more suited to use on horseback, and the [composite bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_bow "Composite bow") enabled mounted archers to use powerful weapons.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-HorseArchery-24)[Seljuk Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seljuk_Turks "Seljuk Turks") used mounted archers against the European [First Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Crusade "First Crusade"), especially at the [Battle of Dorylaeum (1097)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dorylaeum_(1097) "Battle of Dorylaeum (1097)"). One of their tactics was to shoot at the enemy infantry, and use their superior mobility to prevent the enemy from closing with them. Empires throughout the Eurasian landmass often strongly associated their respective "barbarian" counterparts with the usage of the bow and arrow, to the point where powerful states like the [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") referred to their neighbours, the [Xiong-nu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiong-nu "Xiong-nu"), as "Those Who Draw the Bow".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-ChinaEnemies-25) For example, Xiong-nu mounted bowmen made them more than a match for the Han military.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-ChinaEnemies-25) It is possible that "barbarian" peoples were responsible for introducing archery or certain types of bows to their "civilized" counterparts.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-JapanBows-26)

[Native Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") developed a culture of horseback archery after the introduction of the horse by European explorers in the second millennium.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-27)

### Decline of archery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Decline of archery")]

The development of [firearms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpowder_warfare "Gunpowder warfare") rendered the [bow and arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_and_arrow "Bow and arrow") obsolete in warfare, although efforts were sometimes made to preserve archery practice. In England and Wales, for example, the government tried to enforce practice with the longbow until the end of the 16th century.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-28) This was because it was recognized that the bow had been instrumental to military success during the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War "Hundred Years' War"). Despite the high social status, ongoing utility, and widespread pleasure of archery in Armenia, China, Egypt, England and Wales, [the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas"), India, Japan, Korea, Turkey and elsewhere, almost every culture that gained access to even early firearms used them widely, to the neglect of archery. Early firearms were inferior in rate-of-fire, and were very sensitive to wet weather. However, they had longer effective range[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-koreantrad-20) and were tactically superior in the common situation of soldiers shooting at each other from behind obstructions. They also required significantly less training to use properly, in particular penetrating steel armor without any need to develop special musculature. Armies equipped with guns could thus provide superior firepower, and highly trained archers became obsolete on the battlefield. However, the bow and arrow is still an effective weapon, and archers have seen military action in the 21st century.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-31) Traditional archery remains in use for sport, and for hunting in many areas.

### English 18th-century revival as a sport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: English 18th-century revival as a sport")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/The_meeting_of_the_Royal_British_Bowmen_in_the_grounds_of_Erthig%2C_Denbighshire.jpeg/250px-The_meeting_of_the_Royal_British_Bowmen_in_the_grounds_of_Erthig%2C_Denbighshire.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_meeting_of_the_Royal_British_Bowmen_in_the_grounds_of_Erthig,_Denbighshire.jpeg)

A print of the 1822 meeting of the "Royal British Bowmen" archery club.

Early recreational archery societies included the Finsbury Archers in England and the Ancient Society of Kilwinning Archers in Scotland. The latter's annual [Papingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popinjay_(sport) "Popinjay (sport)") event was first recorded in 1483. (In this event, archers shoot vertically from the base of an abbey tower to dislodge a wood pigeon placed approximately 30 m (98 ft) above.)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-32) The Royal Company of Archers was formed in 1676 and is one of the oldest sporting bodies in the world.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-33) Archery remained a small and scattered pastime, however, until the late 18th century when it experienced a fashionable revival among the [aristocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristocracy "Aristocracy"). Sir [Ashton Lever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashton_Lever "Ashton Lever"), an antiquarian and collector, formed the [Toxophilite Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxophilite_Society "Toxophilite Society") in London in 1781, with the patronage of [George, the Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_IV "George IV").

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Archers_by_Adam_Buck_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Archers_by_Adam_Buck_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Archers_by_Adam_Buck_(cropped).jpg)

Fashionable female archers, 1799

Archery societies were set up across the country, each with its own strict entry criteria and outlandish costumes. Recreational archery soon became extravagant social and ceremonial events for the nobility, complete with flags, music and [21-gun salutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21-gun_salute "21-gun salute") for the competitors. The clubs were "the drawing rooms of the great country houses placed outside" and thus came to play an important role in the social networks of the local upper class. As well as its emphasis on display and status, the sport was notable for its popularity with females. Young women could not only compete in the contests but retain and show off their sexuality while doing so. Thus, archery came to act as a forum for introductions, flirtation and romance.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-34) It was often consciously styled in the manner of a [Medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval")[tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tournament "Tournament") with titles and [laurel wreaths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_wreath "Laurel wreath") being presented as a reward to the victor. General meetings were held from 1789, in which local lodges convened together to standardise the rules and ceremonies. Archery was also co-opted as a distinctively British tradition, dating back to the lore of [Robin Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood "Robin Hood") and it served as a patriotic form of entertainment at a time of political tension in Europe. The societies were also elitist, and the new [middle class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_class "Middle class")[bourgeoisie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourgeoisie "Bourgeoisie") were excluded from the clubs due to their lack of social status.

After the [Napoleonic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars "Napoleonic Wars"), the sport became increasingly popular among all classes, and it was framed as a nostalgic reimagining of the [preindustrial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrialisation "Industrialisation") rural Britain. Particularly influential was Sir [Walter Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Scott "Walter Scott")'s 1819 novel, _[Ivanhoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivanhoe "Ivanhoe")_ that depicted the heroic character Lockseley winning an archery tournament.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-35)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Lieksa.vaakuna.svg/250px-Lieksa.vaakuna.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lieksa.vaakuna.svg)

An archery in the coat of arms of [Lieksa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieksa "Lieksa"),[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-36) based on the 1669 seal of the old town of Brahea.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-37)

### A modern sport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: A modern sport")]

The 1840s saw the second attempts at turning the recreation into a modern sport. The first [Grand National Archery Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_National_Archery_Society "Grand National Archery Society") meeting was held in [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York "York") in 1844 and over the next decade the extravagant and festive practices of the past were gradually whittled away and the rules were standardized as the 'York Round' - a series of shoots at 55 m (180 ft), 73 m (240 ft), and 91 m (299 ft). [Horace A. Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_A._Ford "Horace A. Ford") helped to improve archery standards and pioneered new archery techniques. He won the Grand National 11 times in a row and published a highly influential guide to the sport in 1856.

[![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/29/Saxton_Pope_and_grizzly.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saxton_Pope_and_grizzly.jpg)

Picture of [Saxton Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxton_Pope "Saxton Pope") taken while grizzly hunting at Yellowstone

Towards the end of the 19th century, the sport experienced declining participation as alternative sports such as [croquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croquet "Croquet") and [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis") became more popular among the middle class. By 1889, just 50 archery clubs were left in Britain, but it was still included as a sport at the [1900 Paris Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Paris_Olympics "1900 Paris Olympics").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-38)

The National Archery Association of the United States was organized in 1879, in part by [Maurice Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Thompson "Maurice Thompson")[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-39) (the author of the seminal text "[The Witchery of Archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witchery_of_Archery "The Witchery of Archery")") and his brother [Will Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Thompson_(archer) "William Thompson (archer)"). Maurice was president in its inaugural year and Will was president in 1882, 1903, and 1904.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-40) The 1910 President was Frank E Canfield.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-41) Today it is known as USA Archery and is recognized by [United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Olympic_&_Paralympic_Committee "United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-42)

In the United States, primitive archery was revived in the early 20th century. The last of the [Yahi Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahi#Yahi "Yahi") tribe, a native known as [Ishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishi "Ishi"), came out of hiding in California in 1911.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-44) His doctor, [Saxton Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxton_Pope "Saxton Pope"), learned many of Ishi's traditional archery skills, and popularized them.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-46)[_[non-primary source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No\_original\_research#Primary,\_secondary\_and\_tertiary\_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")_]The [Pope and Young Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club "Pope and Young Club"), founded in 1961 and named in honor of Pope and his friend, Arthur Young, became one of North America's leading bowhunting and conservation organizations. Founded as a nonprofit scientific organization, the Club was patterned after the prestigious [Boone and Crockett Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boone_and_Crockett_Club "Boone and Crockett Club") and advocated responsible bowhunting by promoting quality, fair chase hunting, and sound conservation practices.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From the 1920s, professional engineers took an interest in archery, previously the exclusive field of traditional craft experts.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-technical-47) They led the commercial development of new forms of bow including the modern [recurve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurve_bow "Recurve bow") and [compound bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compound_bow "Compound bow"). These modern forms are now dominant in modern Western archery; traditional bows are in a minority. Archery returned to the Olympics in 1972. In the 1980s, the skills of traditional archery were revived by American enthusiasts, and combined with the new scientific understanding. Much of this expertise is available in the _Traditional Bowyer's Bibles_ (see Further reading). Modern game archery owes much of its success to [Fred Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Bear "Fred Bear"), an American bow hunter and bow manufacturer.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-48)

### Mythology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Mythology")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Vishwamitra_archery_training-1.jpg/250px-Vishwamitra_archery_training-1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vishwamitra_archery_training-1.jpg)

[Vishwamitra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vishwamitra "Vishwamitra") archery training from [Ramayana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramayana "Ramayana")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Herakles_the_Archer_-_%C3%89mile_Antoine_Bourdelle_-_ABDAG004586.jpg/250px-Herakles_the_Archer_-_%C3%89mile_Antoine_Bourdelle_-_ABDAG004586.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Herakles_the_Archer_-_%C3%89mile_Antoine_Bourdelle_-_ABDAG004586.jpg)

_Herakles the Archer_ by [Émile Antoine Bourdelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Antoine_Bourdelle "Émile Antoine Bourdelle")

Deities and heroes in several mythologies are described as archers, including the Greek [Artemis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis "Artemis") and [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo "Apollo"), the Roman [Diana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_(mythology) "Diana (mythology)") and [Cupid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupid "Cupid"), the Germanic [Agilaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agilaz "Agilaz"), continuing in legends like those of [Wilhelm Tell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Tell "Wilhelm Tell"), [Palnetoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palnetoke "Palnetoke"), or [Robin Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood "Robin Hood"). Armenian [Hayk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayk "Hayk") and Babylonian [Marduk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marduk "Marduk"), Indian [Karna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karna "Karna") (also known as Radheya/son of Radha), [Abhimanyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abhimanyu "Abhimanyu"), [Eklavya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eklavya "Eklavya"), [Arjuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjuna "Arjuna"), [Bhishma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhishma "Bhishma"), [Drona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drona "Drona"), [Rama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rama "Rama"), and [Shiva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiva "Shiva") were known for their shooting skills. The famous archery competition of hitting the eye of a rotating fish while watching its reflection in the water bowl was one of the many archery skills depicted in the _[Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata")_.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-49) Persian [Arash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arash_(mythology) "Arash (mythology)") was a famous archer. Earlier Greek representations of [Heracles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heracles "Heracles") normally depict him as an archer. Archery, and the bow, play an important part in the epic poem the _Odyssey,_ when Odysseus returns home in disguise and then bests the suitors in an archery competition after hinting at his identity by stringing and drawing his great bow that only he can draw, a similar motif is present in the Turkic Iranian heroic archeheroic poem _Alpamysh_.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-50)

Three of the [Hyperborean Maidens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperborean_maidens "Hyperborean maidens") were worshipped on the Greek island of Delos as attendants of [Artemis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis "Artemis"), presiding over aspects of archery; _Hekaerge_ (Ἑκαέργη), represented distancing, _Loxo_ (Λοξώ), trajectory, and _Oupis_ (Οὖπις), aim.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-51)

[Yi the archer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hou_Yi "Hou Yi") and his apprentice [Feng Meng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feng_Meng "Feng Meng") appear in several early Chinese myths,[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-selby-52) and the historical character of [Zhou Tong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Tong_(archer) "Zhou Tong (archer)") features in many fictional forms. [Jumong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jumong "Jumong"), the first [Taewang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taewang "Taewang") of the [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo") kingdom of the [Three Kingdoms of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Kingdoms_of_Korea "Three Kingdoms of Korea"), is claimed by legend to have been a near-godlike archer. Archery features in the story of Oguz Khagan. Similarly, archery and the bow feature heavily into historical Korean identity.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-53)

In [West African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa "West Africa")[Yoruba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoruba_religion "Yoruba religion") belief, [Osoosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ochosi "Ochosi") is one of several deities of the hunt who are identified with bow and arrow iconography and other insignia associated with archery.

## Equipment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Equipment")]

### Types of bows

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Types of bows")]

Main article: [Bow and arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_and_arrow "Bow and arrow")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Pacific_Yew_Selfbow.jpg/250px-Pacific_Yew_Selfbow.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pacific_Yew_Selfbow.jpg)

A Pacific yew selfbow drawn by the _split finger_ method. Selfbows are made from a single piece of wood.

While there is great variety in the construction details of bows (both historical and modern), all bows consist of a string attached to elastic limbs that store mechanical energy imparted by the user drawing the string. Bows may be broadly split into two categories: those drawn by pulling the string directly and those that use a mechanism to pull the string.

Directly drawn bows may be further divided based upon differences in the method of limb construction, notable examples being [self bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self_bow "Self bow"), [laminated bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laminated_bow "Laminated bow"), and [composite bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_bow "Composite bow"). Bows can also be classified by the [bow shape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape "Shape") of the limbs when unstrung; in contrast to traditional European straight bows, a [recurve bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurve_bow#Recurve_bow "Recurve bow") and some types of longbow have tips that curve away from the archer when the bow is unstrung. The cross-section of the limb also varies; the classic [longbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbow "Longbow") is a tall bow with narrow limbs that are D-shaped in cross section, and the [flatbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flatbow "Flatbow") has flat wide limbs that are approximately rectangular in cross-section. [Cable-backed bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable-backed_bow "Cable-backed bow") use cords as the back of the bow; the draw weight of the bow can be adjusted by changing the tension of the cable. They were widespread among [Inuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inuit "Inuit") who lacked easy access to good bow wood. One variety of cable-backed bow is the Penobscot bow or [Wabenaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wabenaki "Wabenaki") bow, invented by Frank Loring (Chief Big Thunder) about 1900.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-54) It consists of a small bow attached by cables on the back of a larger main bow.

In different cultures, the arrows are released from either the left or right side of the bow, and this affects the hand grip and position of the bow. In [Arab archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_archery "Arab archery"), [Turkish archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_archery "Turkish archery"), and [Japanese archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ky%C5%ABd%C5%8D "Kyūdō"). The arrows are released from the right hand side of the bow, and this affects construction of the bow. In western archery, the arrow is usually released from the left hand side of the bow for a right-handed archer.

[Compound bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compound_bow "Compound bow") are designed to reduce the force required to hold the string at full draw, hence allowing the archer more time to aim with less muscular stress. Most compound designs use cams or elliptical wheels on the ends of the limbs to achieve this. A typical let-off is anywhere from 65% to 80%. For example, a 27 kg (60 lb) bow with 80% let-off only requires 53 N (12 lb f) to hold at full draw. Up to 99% let-off is possible.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-55) The compound bow was invented by [Holless Wilbur Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holless_Wilbur_Allen "Holless Wilbur Allen") in the 1960s (a US patent was filed in 1966 and granted in 1969) and it has become the most widely used type of bow for all forms of archery in North America.

Mechanically drawn bows typically have a stock or other mounting, such as the [crossbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossbow "Crossbow"). Crossbows typically have shorter draw lengths compared to compound bows. Because of this, heavier draw weights are required to achieve the same energy transfer to the arrow. These mechanically drawn bows also have devices to hold the tension when the bow is fully drawn. They are not limited by the strength of a single archer and larger varieties have been used as [siege engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engine "Siege engine").

### Types of arrows and fletchings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Types of arrows and fletchings")]

Main article: [Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow "Arrow")

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Brazilarcher.jpg/250px-Brazilarcher.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brazilarcher.jpg)

A [Rikbaktsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rikbaktsa "Rikbaktsa") archer competes at Brazil's Indigenous Games

The most common form of arrow consists of a [shaft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow_straightener "Arrow straightener"), with an [arrowhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrowhead "Arrowhead") at the front end, and [fletchings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fletching "Fletching") and a [nock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow#Nocks "Arrow") at the other end. Arrows across time and history have normally been carried in a container known as a [quiver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiver "Quiver"), which can take many different forms. Shafts of arrows are typically composed of solid [wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood "Wood"), [bamboo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamboo "Bamboo"), [fiberglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass-reinforced_plastic "Glass-reinforced plastic"), [aluminium alloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_alloy "Aluminium alloy"), [carbon fiber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fiber "Carbon fiber"), or [composite materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_material "Composite material"). Wooden arrows are prone to warping. Fiberglass arrows are brittle, but can be produced to uniform specifications easily. Aluminium shafts were a very popular high-performance choice in the latter half of the 20th century, due to their straightness, lighter weight, and subsequently higher speed and flatter trajectories. Carbon fiber arrows became popular in the 1990s because they are very light, flying even faster and flatter than aluminium arrows. Today, the most popular arrows at tournaments and Olympic events are made of composite materials.

The arrowhead is the primary functional component of the arrow. Some arrows may simply use a sharpened tip of the solid shaft, but separate arrowheads are far more common, usually made from metal, stone, or other hard materials. The most commonly used forms are target points, field points, and broadheads, although there are also other types, such as bodkin, judo, and blunt heads.

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Spliced_feather_0002.jpg/250px-Spliced_feather_0002.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spliced_feather_0002.jpg)

Shield cut straight fletching – here the hen [feathers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feather "Feather") are barred red

[Fletching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fletching "Fletching") is traditionally made from bird feathers, but solid plastic vanes and thin sheet-like spin vanes are used. They are attached near the nock (rear) end of the arrow with thin double sided tape, glue, or, traditionally, sinew. The most common configuration in all cultures is three fletches, though as many as six have been used. Two makes the arrow unstable in flight. When the arrow is _three-fletched_, the fletches are equally spaced around the shaft, with one placed such that it is perpendicular to the bow when nocked on the string, though variations are seen with modern equipment, especially when using the modern spin vanes. This fletch is called the "index fletch" or "cock feather" (also known as "the odd vane out" or "the nocking vane"), and the others are sometimes called the "hen feathers". Commonly, the cock feather is of a different color. However, if archers are using fletching made of feather or similar material, they may use same color vanes, as different dyes can give varying stiffness to vanes, resulting in less precision. When an arrow is _four-fletched_, two opposing fletches are often cock feathers, and occasionally the fletches are not evenly spaced.

The fletching may be either _parabolic_ cut (short feathers in a smooth parabolic curve) or _shield_ cut (generally shaped like half of a narrow shield), and is often attached at an angle, known as _helical_ fletching, to introduce a stabilizing spin to the arrow while in flight. Whether helical or straight fletched, when natural fletching (bird feathers) is used it is critical that all feathers come from the same side of the bird. Oversized fletchings can be used to accentuate drag and thus limit the range of the arrow significantly; these arrows are called _[flu-flus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flu-flu\_arrow "Flu-flu arrow")_. Misplacement of fletchings can change the arrow's flight path dramatically.

### Bowstring

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Bowstring")]

Main article: [Bowstring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowstring "Bowstring")

[Dacron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacron "Dacron") and other modern materials offer high strength for their weight and are used on most modern bows. Linen and other traditional materials are still used on traditional bows. Several modern methods of making a bowstring exist, such as the 'endless loop' and 'Flemish twist'. Almost any fiber can be made into a bowstring. The author of _Arab Archery_ suggests the hide of a young, emaciated camel.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-arabarchery-56)[Njál's saga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nj%C3%A1l's_saga "Njál's saga") describes the refusal of a wife, Hallgerður, to cut her hair to make an emergency bowstring for her husband, [Gunnar Hámundarson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunnar_H%C3%A1mundarson "Gunnar Hámundarson"), who is then killed.

### Protective equipment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Protective equipment")]

Main articles: [Bracer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bracer "Bracer"), [Finger tab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finger_tab "Finger tab"), and [Thumb ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thumb_ring "Thumb ring")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Finger-tab_hg.jpg/250px-Finger-tab_hg.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Finger-tab_hg.jpg)

A right-hand finger tab to protect the hand while the string is drawn

Most modern archers wear a [bracer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bracer_(archery) "Bracer (archery)") (also known as an arm-guard) to protect the inside of the bow arm from being hit by the string and prevent clothing from catching the bowstring. The bracer does not brace the arm; the word comes from the armoury term "[brassard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brassard "Brassard")", meaning an armoured sleeve or badge. The [Navajo people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navajo_people "Navajo people") have developed highly ornamented bracers as non-functional items of adornment.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-ketoh-57) Some archers (nearly all female archers) wear protection on their chests, called chestguards or plastrons. The myth of the [Amazons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazons "Amazons") was that they had one breast removed to solve this problem.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-58)[Roger Ascham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ascham "Roger Ascham") mentions one archer, presumably with an unusual shooting style, who wore a leather guard for his face.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-ascham-59)

The drawing digits are normally protected by a leather [tab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finger_tab "Finger tab"), glove, or [thumb ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thumb_ring "Thumb ring"). A simple tab of leather is commonly used, as is a skeleton glove. Medieval Europeans probably used a complete leather glove.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-warbow-60)

Eurasiatic archers who used the thumb or Mongolian draw protected their thumbs, usually with leather according to the author of _Arab Archery_,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-61) but also with [special rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thumb_ring "Thumb ring") of various hard materials. Many surviving Turkish and Chinese examples are works of considerable art. Some are so highly ornamented that the users could not have used them to loose an arrow. Possibly these were items of personal adornment, and hence value, remaining extant whilst leather had virtually no intrinsic value and would also deteriorate with time. In traditional [Japanese archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ky%C5%ABd%C5%8D "Kyūdō") a special [glove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugake "Yugake") is used that has a ridge to assist in drawing the string.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-Elmer_R.P._pages_345-349-62)

### Release aids

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Release aids")]

Main article: [Release aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Release_aid "Release aid")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Release-aid.jpg/250px-Release-aid.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Release-aid.jpg)

Release aid

A release aid is a mechanical device designed to give a crisp and precise loose of arrows from a compound bow. In the most commonly used, the string is released by a finger-operated trigger mechanism, held in the archer's hand or attached to their wrist. In another type, known as a back-tension release, the string is automatically released when drawn to a pre-determined tension.

### Stabilizers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Stabilizers")]

Main article: [Stabiliser (archery)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stabiliser_(archery) "Stabiliser (archery)")

Stabilizers are mounted at various points on the bow. Common with competitive archery equipment are special brackets that allow multiple stabilizers to be mounted at various angles to fine tune the bow's balance.

Stabilizers aid in aiming by improving the balance of the bow. Sights, quivers, rests, and design of the riser (the central, non-bending part of the bow) make one side of the bow heavier. One purpose of stabilizers are to offset these forces. A reflex riser design will cause the top limb to lean towards the shooter. In this case a heavier front stabilizer is desired to offset this action. A deflex riser design has the opposite effect and a lighter front stabilizer may be used.

Stabilizers can reduce noise and vibration. These energies are absorbed by viscoelastic polymers, gels, powders, and other materials used to build stabilizers.

Stabilizers improve the forgiveness and accuracy by increasing the moment of inertia of the bow to resist movement during the shooting process. Lightweight carbon stabilizers with weighted ends are desirable because they improve the moment of inertia while minimizing the weight added.

## Shooting technique and form

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archery&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Shooting technique and form")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Mediaeval_archery_reenactment.jpg/250px-Mediaeval_archery_reenactment.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mediaeval_archery_reenactment.jpg)

[Historical reenactment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_reenactment "Historical reenactment") of medieval archery

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Thrill_of_the_hunt.jpg/250px-Thrill_of_the_hunt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Thrill_of_the_hunt.jpg)

Chief Master Sgt. Kevin Peterson demonstrates safe archery techniques while aiming an arrow at a target on the 28th Force Support Squadron trap and skeet range at [Ellsworth Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellsworth_Air_Force_Base "Ellsworth Air Force Base"), S.D., 11 October 2012.

The standard convention on teaching archery is to hold the bow depending upon eye dominance.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-63) (One exception is in modern [kyūdō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ky%C5%ABd%C5%8D "Kyūdō") where all archers are trained to hold the bow in the left hand.)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery#cite_note-64) Therefore, if one is right-eye dominant, they would hold the bow in the left hand and draw the string with the right hand. However, not everyone agrees with this line of thought. A smoother, and more fluid release of the string will produce the most consistently repeatable shots, and therefore may provide greater accuracy of the arrow flight. Some believe that the hand with the greatest dexterity should therefore be the hand that draws and releases the string. Either eye can be used for aiming, and the less dominant eye can be trained over time to become more effective for use. To assist with this, an eye patch can be temporarily worn over the dominant eye.

The hand that holds the bow is referred to as the _bow hand_ and its arm the _bow arm_. The opposite hand is called the _drawing hand_ or _string hand_. Terms such as _bow shoulder_ or _string elbow_ follow the same convention.

If shooting according to eye dominance, right-eye-dominant archers shooting conventionally hold the bow with their left hand. If shooting according to hand dexterity, the archer draws the string with the hand that possesses the greatest dexterity, regardless of eye dominance.
