**Charles Elbert Grayson** (July 24, 1910 – May 17, 2009) was an [archer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery"), [bowyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowyer "Bowyer"), archery collector, and [author](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Author "Author"). His archery collection is contained in the [University of Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Missouri "University of Missouri") Museum of Anthropology.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_E._Grayson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Charles Grayson was born in 1910 on a farm in Iowa, the eighth in a family of nine children. When he was nine years old, the family relocated to Riverside, California. He graduated from Riverside Polytechnic High School in 1928 and from there, went on to attend [Pomona College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomona_College "Pomona College") from 1928 to 1933. While attending Pomona College he and a friend, together with a Japanese student, began archery as a sport. This was Grayson's first introduction to formal Japanese archery. After graduation from Pomona, Grayson studied physics at the University of California, Berkeley, but eventually changed his interests to medicine. He graduated from Stanford School of Medicine in 1942 as a radiologist.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-1)

## Interest in archery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_E._Grayson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Interest in archery")]

A close neighbor of Grayson's in Riverside, a scoutmaster and archer, was friends with prominent archers such as Art Young, [Saxton Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxton_Pope "Saxton Pope"), and [William "Chief" Compton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_%22Chief%22_Compton?action=edit&redlink=1 "William \"Chief\" Compton (page does not exist)"). Grayson made his first bow from a [lemonwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xymalos_monospora "Xymalos monospora") stave that he won selling tickets to a movie about Art Young's trek across Alaska.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-2)

In private practice in Sacramento, Grayson took up archery again. He became skilled in making various types of bows and became involved in local, regional, and national archery associations. He has won many medals in competition, at one time holding the amateur record for the 65-lb class in flight shooting. Hunting expeditions and professional travel provided opportunities to collect archery-related materials in areas such as Mexico, British Columbia, Alaska, and Africa.

In 1960, Grayson and his wife built a house in Oregon where they retired in 1972. There he added a building to house his vast archery collection and related materials like [thumb rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thumb_rings?action=edit&redlink=1 "Thumb rings (page does not exist)"), ivory sculpture, and paintings. He began donating his collection to the University of Missouri Museum of Anthropology in the early 1990s.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-3)

## Archery Collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_E._Grayson&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Archery Collection")]

Dr. Grayson collected [archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery") from all over the world. His archery collection spans artifacts from [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet"), [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea "Korea"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [Mongolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolia "Mongolia"), the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines"), [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa"), [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America"), as well as more contemporary pieces from [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") ([England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England")) as well as the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-4) Dr. Grayson also collected bows from [Fred Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Bear "Fred Bear") and collected many of the record setting flight bows from [Harry Drake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Drake "Harry Drake"). [[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-5)

## Academic career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_E._Grayson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Academic career")]

In addition to being an avid collector of archery and archery related objects, Dr. Grayson also researched and published on archery topics. Many of his articles appeared in the magazine, [Primitive Archer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_Archer?action=edit&redlink=1 "Primitive Archer (page does not exist)"). _Shear_, for example,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-6) discussed the effects of shear in the construction of both [self bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self_bows?action=edit&redlink=1 "Self bows (page does not exist)") and [composite bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_bows "Composite bows"). He also wrote a variety of articles about archery traditions from around the world such as, _Somali Archery_,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-7)_Eskimo Bows, Arrows, and Quivers_[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-8) and _Wintu Archery_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-9)

> Most collectors today have either directly or indirectly benefited from Bert's discoveries and finds. Very few people realize however just how generous and helpful he has been to these other collectors over the years. He has made these contributions anonymously, and without an inflated ego. Hopefully that anonymity will become lost at the museum in Missouri and in his upcoming book. What's more he is the only collector alive who spent more than a year traveling around the world, from continent to continent, collecting and documenting his finds. If history teaches any lessons at all, Bert will be remembered as the one individual in our time who preserved treasures of the past, which would have otherwise been completely lost or forgotten. I am confident future generations will realize the value of his work even more than today

—Jack B. Harrison, Primitive Archer Magazine, Volume 11, Issue 2

[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-10)

Grayson was a member as well as Vice President of the [Society of Archer-Antiquaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Archer-Antiquaries?action=edit&redlink=1 "Society of Archer-Antiquaries (page does not exist)").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-11)

He was an inductee in the [Archery Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery_Hall_of_Fame "Archery Hall of Fame") in 2005.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-12)

# Will Thompson

[![Image 2](https://olympedia-photos.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/2249.jpg)](https://olympedia-photos.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/2249.jpg "Photo of Will Thompson")

## Biographical information

| Sex | Male |
| Full name | William Henry "Will"•Thompson |
| Used name | Will•Thompson |
| Born | 10 March 1848 in [Calhoun, Georgia (USA)](https://www.olympedia.org/place_names/17866) |
| Died | 10 August 1918 (aged 70 years 5 months) in [Seattle, Washington (USA)](https://www.olympedia.org/place_names/2782) |
| Affiliations | [Potomac Archers, Washington (USA)](https://www.olympedia.org/affiliations/7636) |

**Medals**OG

## Biography

Born in the state of Georgia, Will Thompson was educated at the Georgia Military Institute and at the age of sixteen enlisted in the Confederate army for service in the American Civil War. He was in the campaign of the Wilderness, the battles of Spottsylvania Court House, Cold Harbor and Petersburg and served through to the end of the war. He was a civil engineer, working in railroad and canal construction before being called to the bar in 1872. He practiced law, firstly in a partnership with his brother Maurice, and later as personal attorney for the railroad tycoon James J. Hill. Supposedly inspired by his friend and neighbour, Lew Wallace, the author of “Ben Hur”, he took up writing and was a regular contributor to literary magazines for the rest of his life. His most famous poem “The High Tide at Gettysburg” is considered one of the finest works of Civil War poetry. In 1907 two strands of his life came together when, quoting from “High Tide at Gettysburg” in a closing address which was reported as having both judge and jury in tears, he defended his own son on a charge of first degree murder. The case ended in an acquittal on the grounds of insanity. Along with his brother Maurice, he was one of the founders of The American Archery Association in 1878 and was to win the national championship on five occasions between 1879 and 1908.

Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://wikimediafoundation.org/annualreports/current/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

11% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

**Bear Archery** is a manufacturer and marketer of bows and archery equipment located in [Gainesville, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gainesville,_Florida "Gainesville, Florida"), owned by [Escalade Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escalade_Sports "Escalade Sports").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Archery#cite_note-1)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bear_Archery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The company was founded in 1933 as the _Bear Products Company_ in [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit"), Michigan by [Fred Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Bear "Fred Bear") and Charles Piper.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Archery#cite_note-2) The initial focus was on [silk-screening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk-screening "Silk-screening") and advertising support work for automotive companies.

In 1938 Fred Bear hired Nels Grumley, a woodworker and [bowyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowyer "Bowyer"), and the company expanded to offer hand-made bows.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Archery#cite_note-3)

Fred Bear sold the advertising side of the Bear Products Company in 1940. The archery business was named Bear Archery.

In 1947 the company moved to a new facility in [Grayling, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grayling,_Michigan "Grayling, Michigan"). The Grayling plant focused on making and marketing [recurve bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurve_bow "Recurve bow") and [longbows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbow "Longbow") in a growing archery market. Bow manufacturing changed from hand-made bows to mass production using [fiberglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiberglass "Fiberglass") and other modern materials.

Fred Bear sold the company to Victor Comptometer in 1968,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Archery#cite_note-Rappe-4) but remained the president of Bear Archery. The company was not one of the first [compound bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compound_bow "Compound bow") manufacturers, but eventually found success with early models like the Whitetail Hunter. Bear Archery moved manufacturing from Michigan to Gainesville, Florida in 1978.

Over the next three decades Bear Archery changed hands in a series of mergers, acquisitions, and spin-offs from Victor Comptometer to Walter Kidde & Co,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Archery#cite_note-5) Hanson PLC, U.S. Industries,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Archery#cite_note-6) Fenway Partners[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Archery#cite_note-7) and the North American Archery Group. All Bear archery products are being produced in Gainesville, Florida.

In 2003 [Escalade Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escalade_Sports "Escalade Sports") acquired the North American Archery Group and currently does business as Bear Archery Inc.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Archery#cite_note-8)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American hunter and physician

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9f/Dr._Saxton_Pope.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dr._Saxton_Pope.jpg)

Dr. Saxton Pope

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/29/Saxton_Pope_and_grizzly.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saxton_Pope_and_grizzly.jpg)

Picture of Pope taken while grizzly hunting at Yellowstone

**Saxton Temple Pope** (September 4, 1875 – August 8, 1926) was an American doctor, teacher, author and outdoorsman. He is most famous as the father of modern [bow hunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_hunting "Bow hunting"), and for his close relationship with [Ishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishi "Ishi"), the last member of the [Yahi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahi "Yahi") tribe and the last known [American Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") to be raised largely isolated from Western culture.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-bio-1)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saxton_Pope&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Born in [Fort Stockton, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Stockton,_Texas "Fort Stockton, Texas") as the son of an army surgeon, Pope grew up in military camps and frontier towns, where he learned outdoor skills and became an athlete. This is where he first learned archery, as well as horsemanship, riflery, knifemaking, and other skills. He built and attempted to fly a glider.

He later went to medical school at the [University of California, Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley") graduating in 1899. He set up a practice in [Watsonville, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watsonville,_California "Watsonville, California") near San Francisco, married Emma Wightman, a medical school classmate, and had four children. In 1912, he became a surgical instructor at the medical school.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-bio-1)

## Relationship with Ishi

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saxton_Pope&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Relationship with Ishi")]

The medical school where Pope taught was located near the [museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoebe_A._Hearst_Museum_of_Anthropology "Phoebe A. Hearst Museum of Anthropology") where Ishi worked as a janitor, having been brought there for study by Professor [T. T. Waterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._T._Waterman "T. T. Waterman") of the [University of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California "University of California") Department of Anthropology. Because Ishi had grown up in the isolated Yahi tribe, he had little immunity to diseases, and Pope met Ishi during his stays at the University hospital. Pope learned some of the Yahi language, and spent much time with Ishi, learning of his life and listening to the Yahi tribal folklore. Ishi taught Pope how to make bows and arrows as the Yahi did, and how to hunt with them. Pope and Ishi remained close until Ishi's death from [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis") in 1916.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-2) In spite of this close relationship and against Ishi's frequently stated wishes, Pope insisted that Ishi be autopsied after death and his brain removed.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-3)

## Later life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saxton_Pope&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life")]

Pope became an avid bowhunter during his time with Ishi, and he continued that after Ishi's death. In 1920, with special permission, Pope and a companion, Arthur Young, went hunting [grizzly bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grizzly_bear "Grizzly bear") in [Yellowstone National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_National_Park "Yellowstone National Park") with hand made bows and steel tipped arrows, taking several. The stuffed and mounted bears are on display at the California Academy of Sciences.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-bio-1) Pope later wrote a book, _Hunting with the Bow and Arrow_, which remains in print. He continued bowhunting until his death in 1926 from [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-bio-1)

Hunting by archery

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/171114-F-LS255-0011.JPG/330px-171114-F-LS255-0011.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:171114-F-LS255-0011.JPG)

Bowhunter in [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah")

**Bowhunting** (or **bow hunting**) is the practice of [hunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunting "Hunting")[game animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_(food) "Game (food)") by [archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery"). Many [indigenous peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples "Indigenous peoples") have employed the technique as their primary hunting method for thousands of years, and it has survived into contemporary use for sport and hunting.

## Modern history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Modern history")]

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/29/Saxton_Pope_and_grizzly.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saxton_Pope_and_grizzly.jpg)

Picture of Pope taken while [grizzly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grizzly_bear "Grizzly bear") hunting at [Yellowstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_National_Park "Yellowstone National Park")

The last of the [Yahi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahi#Yahi "Yahi") tribe, an indigenous man known as [Ishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishi "Ishi"), came out of hiding in California in 1911.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-2) His doctor, [Saxton Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxton_Pope "Saxton Pope"), learned many of Ishi's traditional archery skills, and popularized them.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-4) The [Pope and Young Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club "Pope and Young Club"), founded in 1961 and named in honor of Pope and his friend, Arthur Young, became one of North America's leading bowhunting and conservation organizations. Founded as a nonprofit scientific organization, the club was patterned after the [Boone and Crockett Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boone_and_Crockett_Club "Boone and Crockett Club") and advocated responsible bowhunting by promoting quality, [fair chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_chase "Fair chase") hunting, and sound conservation practices. Modern game archery owes much of its success to [Fred Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Bear "Fred Bear"), an American bow hunter and bow manufacturer.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-Bertalan2007-5)

## Equipment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Equipment")]

[Arrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow "Arrow"), [bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_(weapon) "Bow (weapon)") and [sights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sights "Sights") are commonly of the more modern varieties. However, all effective variations, including [crossbows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossbow "Crossbow") and [wooden bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self_bow "Self bow") launching wooden arrows with stone points, are used. [Arrowheads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrowhead "Arrowhead") are chosen to ensure lethality. Broadheads feature blades that jut out from the shaft at an angle to cause more damage to the target; some models have retractable blades that only deploy once they hit the target.

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Crossbow_Hunting.jpg/250px-Crossbow_Hunting.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crossbow_Hunting.jpg)

Hunting [crossbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossbow "Crossbow")

Big game hunting requires a draw weight of more than 35 [pounds-force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_(force) "Pound (force)") (16 [kilograms-force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilogram-force "Kilogram-force")). For larger game such as elk or moose, more than 50 lbf (23 kgf) is suggested. Most male American archers can draw a bow rated at 50–60 lbf (23–27 kgf), most women 30–40 lbf (14–18 kgf).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-6)

Lighter arrows, all else equal, will give a higher speed and a flatter trajectory.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-7) Arrows with greater mass carry more [momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momentum "Momentum"), and penetrate better in large animals; a minimum mass of 650 [grains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grain_(unit) "Grain (unit)") (40 [grams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram "Gram")) is recommended for animals such as deer, pigs, etc. and 900 gr (60 g) for the largest game.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-8)

## Methods of hunting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Methods of hunting")]

In contrast to a rifle hunter, who may shoot effectively from ranges in excess of 200 yards (180 m); archers usually restrict shots to 2.3 to 42 yards (2 to 38 m).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-9) The distance depends upon individual ability, the target animal, the bow strength, terrain, arrow and weather. The bow hunter may walk along the ground slowly, looking for game and stalking it carefully in the final approach. This type of slow, methodical stalking, is called "spot and stalk." Hunters often wear [camouflage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camouflage "Camouflage") clothing and walk upwind (with the wind in their face) so that game ahead of them cannot smell them.

In "stand hunting," the hunter waits for game to come to them, usually near food, water, or known trails. Brush and other natural materials may be placed for cover, or a "ground blind" that looks like a camouflage tent may be used.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-Woodrow-10) They usually "pop" up and can be set up from folded in a few minutes. The hunter may wait on a wooden or metal stand elevated in a tree, from three to six meters (3.5 to 6.5 yd).

Bowhunting for fish is called [bowfishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowfishing "Bowfishing"). Bowfishing equipment usually adds a line attached to a spool or a reel as well as a specially designed, heavier, barbed arrow. Most bow-fishers do not use sights, but if they do have sights they are different from standard ones to allow for [refraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refraction "Refraction").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-11)

## Legal and cultural considerations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Legal and cultural considerations")]

Bowhunting often has different seasons and restrictions from firearm hunting, and they differ significantly between areas. Legal and cultural approaches specific to the area must be taken into consideration by the hunter.

### Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Europe")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Bogenjagd_in_Europa.png/250px-Bogenjagd_in_Europa.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bogenjagd_in_Europa.png)

Legal status of bowhunting in Europe with countries allowing bowhunting in green

Nations including Denmark, France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Hungary, Finland and Bulgaria use bow and arrow hunting as a hunting tool in modern game management. Some European countries, including the United Kingdom, prohibit bowhunting.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-12) Bowhunting, like target archery, was revived in the UK during the Victorian era,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-13) but has been banned since 1965.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-14) Recently a law was passed in [Estonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonia "Estonia") that would allow bowhunting of [small game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_game "Small game").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-15)

### United States and Canada

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: United States and Canada")]

In the United States and Canada, as with other styles of hunting, bowhunting is regulated by individual provinces and states. Regulations often address issues such as which area to hunt in, what time of year (season), and which sex and species of game may be taken. In many cases, a special archery season is set aside, to minimize interference from rifle hunters. While bowhunting can run into rifle hunting seasons, hunter orange is typically required to be worn during the cross over seasons. In addition, in an effort to maximize game recovery and shot lethality, there are often technical regulations, such as a minimum draw weight, minimum width of head, and lack of barbs.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-16)

In general most bow hunting for big game begins in late August or early September in northern states and Canadian provinces, and slightly later in southern states.

### New Zealand

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: New Zealand")]

Organized bow hunting began in New Zealand in 1945. The New Zealand government regulates bowhunting.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-NZ_REG-17) An annual 3 day field shoot tournament is held every king's birthday weekend at various locations throughout New Zealand. Bowhunters must have permission to hunt on private land, and they cannot hunt in DOC lands, national parks, or any other reserves without a permit. All native species are protected; only introduced species are legal quarry.

There are no special seasons for bowhunters or for hunting with a firearm.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-NZ_DOC-18) There is an active bow hunters' society.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-NZ_BS-19)

### Australia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Australia")]

Bowhunting is practiced in Australia and is not specifically subject to regulation by law. Only non-native species are recognized as game by the Australian Bowhunters Association. However, native species may be killed during government-authorized culls.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-20)

The states of [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_(Australia) "Victoria (Australia)") and [New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales "New South Wales") both regulate bowhunting. In Victoria hunting is regulated through the Department of Sustainability and Environment (DSE).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-VIC_DSE-21) In New South Wales this is done through the Department of Primary Industry.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-NSW_GC-22) At the current time there are no specific hunting regulations in other states and territories.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-ABA-23)

In July 2013 the New South Wales Government disbanded the Game Council, and temporarily suspended licensed hunting in NSW State forests.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-NSW_ABO_GC-24)

While both Victoria and New South Wales place licensing requirements on would-be bowhunters, the sport is self-regulated. The Australian Bowhunters Association and local clubs assess hunters through the Bowhunter Proficiency Certificate (BPC) which is designed to ensure that animals are killed according to humane principles.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-BPC-25)

### Zimbabwe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Zimbabwe")]

Zimbabwe has legally permitted hunting with compound bows since 1989 as an exception, and since 1999 under formal legislation. Minimum arrow weights and bow draws are mandated. Bowhunting is only allowed on private or tribal lands, but not in national parks. Bowhunters must be accompanied by licensed guides or professional hunters.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-26) Bowhunting of elephants is mostly conducted in Zimbabwe.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-27) Following international outrage over the [killing of Cecil the lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Cecil_the_lion "Killing of Cecil the lion") in 2015, the Parks and Wildlife Management Authority banned all bowhunting unless specifically authorized as well as other hunting restrictions.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-28)

## Opposition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Opposition")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Newport20230330.jpg/250px-Newport20230330.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Newport20230330.jpg)

Duck in [Newport Beach, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Beach,_California "Newport Beach, California") injured by arrow

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/CDOW20101109.jpg/250px-CDOW20101109.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CDOW20101109.jpg)

Duck injured by crossbow arrows in [Colorado Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Springs,_Colorado "Colorado Springs, Colorado")

Some are deeply opposed to bow hunting in particular, on the grounds of cruelty. The organization [People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_for_the_Ethical_Treatment_of_Animals "People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals") states that "quick kills are rare, and many animals suffer prolonged, painful deaths when hunters severely injure but fail to kill them."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-29)

### Wounding rates

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Wounding rates")]

A study conducted by the [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma") Fish and Wildlife Agencies found that approximately 50% of deer that were shot were never recovered, noting that this rate was similar to data from other studies. Some deer survived for up to 5–7 days before succumbing to their wounds. "71% to 82% of all shots taken" miss the target[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-30) and "shot placement is, for all practical purposes, random".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-31)

In another study from [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"), archers who had passed a pre-season accuracy test claimed that 82% of deer hit were recovered within 24 hours.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-32)

Danish licensed bowhunters are required to complete a report every time that they kill a [roe deer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe_deer "Roe deer"). (To become a licensed bowhunter in [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") it is necessary to pass a very demanding proficiency test, including a test of accuracy in which five of six arrows must hit within the vital area of game targets ranging from roe deer to pheasant in size at unknown distances up to 25 meters (27 yd). Only 2% of Danish bowhunters use traditional equipment.) For 1999–2004, these reports showed that 576 arrows were released at roe deer. 92.5% of these shots resulted in a dead roe deer being collected by the hunter, and 2.6% are documented as misses. In 5% of reports the deer was hit and wounded (as indicated by bodily fluids on the ground or on the arrow), but not recovered by the hunter. The European Bowhunters Association states that "this percentage compares favorably with other means of harvesting roe deer in Europe."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-33)

**Charles Elbert Grayson** (July 24, 1910 – May 17, 2009) was an [archer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery"), [bowyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowyer "Bowyer"), archery collector, and [author](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Author "Author"). His archery collection is contained in the [University of Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Missouri "University of Missouri") Museum of Anthropology.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_E._Grayson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Charles Grayson was born in 1910 on a farm in Iowa, the eighth in a family of nine children. When he was nine years old, the family relocated to Riverside, California. He graduated from Riverside Polytechnic High School in 1928 and from there, went on to attend [Pomona College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomona_College "Pomona College") from 1928 to 1933. While attending Pomona College he and a friend, together with a Japanese student, began archery as a sport. This was Grayson's first introduction to formal Japanese archery. After graduation from Pomona, Grayson studied physics at the University of California, Berkeley, but eventually changed his interests to medicine. He graduated from Stanford School of Medicine in 1942 as a radiologist.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-1)

## Interest in archery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_E._Grayson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Interest in archery")]

A close neighbor of Grayson's in Riverside, a scoutmaster and archer, was friends with prominent archers such as Art Young, [Saxton Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxton_Pope "Saxton Pope"), and [William "Chief" Compton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_%22Chief%22_Compton?action=edit&redlink=1 "William \"Chief\" Compton (page does not exist)"). Grayson made his first bow from a [lemonwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xymalos_monospora "Xymalos monospora") stave that he won selling tickets to a movie about Art Young's trek across Alaska.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-2)

In private practice in Sacramento, Grayson took up archery again. He became skilled in making various types of bows and became involved in local, regional, and national archery associations. He has won many medals in competition, at one time holding the amateur record for the 65-lb class in flight shooting. Hunting expeditions and professional travel provided opportunities to collect archery-related materials in areas such as Mexico, British Columbia, Alaska, and Africa.

In 1960, Grayson and his wife built a house in Oregon where they retired in 1972. There he added a building to house his vast archery collection and related materials like [thumb rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thumb_rings?action=edit&redlink=1 "Thumb rings (page does not exist)"), ivory sculpture, and paintings. He began donating his collection to the University of Missouri Museum of Anthropology in the early 1990s.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-3)

## Archery Collection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_E._Grayson&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Archery Collection")]

Dr. Grayson collected [archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery") from all over the world. His archery collection spans artifacts from [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet"), [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea "Korea"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [Mongolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolia "Mongolia"), the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines"), [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa"), [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America"), as well as more contemporary pieces from [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") ([England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England")) as well as the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-4) Dr. Grayson also collected bows from [Fred Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Bear "Fred Bear") and collected many of the record setting flight bows from [Harry Drake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Drake "Harry Drake"). [[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-5)

## Academic career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_E._Grayson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Academic career")]

In addition to being an avid collector of archery and archery related objects, Dr. Grayson also researched and published on archery topics. Many of his articles appeared in the magazine, [Primitive Archer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_Archer?action=edit&redlink=1 "Primitive Archer (page does not exist)"). _Shear_, for example,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-6) discussed the effects of shear in the construction of both [self bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self_bows?action=edit&redlink=1 "Self bows (page does not exist)") and [composite bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_bows "Composite bows"). He also wrote a variety of articles about archery traditions from around the world such as, _Somali Archery_,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-7)_Eskimo Bows, Arrows, and Quivers_[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-8) and _Wintu Archery_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-9)

> Most collectors today have either directly or indirectly benefited from Bert's discoveries and finds. Very few people realize however just how generous and helpful he has been to these other collectors over the years. He has made these contributions anonymously, and without an inflated ego. Hopefully that anonymity will become lost at the museum in Missouri and in his upcoming book. What's more he is the only collector alive who spent more than a year traveling around the world, from continent to continent, collecting and documenting his finds. If history teaches any lessons at all, Bert will be remembered as the one individual in our time who preserved treasures of the past, which would have otherwise been completely lost or forgotten. I am confident future generations will realize the value of his work even more than today

—Jack B. Harrison, Primitive Archer Magazine, Volume 11, Issue 2

[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-10)

Grayson was a member as well as Vice President of the [Society of Archer-Antiquaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Archer-Antiquaries?action=edit&redlink=1 "Society of Archer-Antiquaries (page does not exist)").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-11)

He was an inductee in the [Archery Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery_Hall_of_Fame "Archery Hall of Fame") in 2005.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_E._Grayson#cite_note-12)

Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://wikimediafoundation.org/annualreports/current/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

11% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/%22The_Witchery_of_Archery%22_by_Maurice_Thomson_book_cover.png/250px-%22The_Witchery_of_Archery%22_by_Maurice_Thomson_book_cover.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%22The_Witchery_of_Archery%22_by_Maurice_Thomson_book_cover.png)

Front cover of _The Witchery of Archery_

_**The Witchery of Archery**_, written by [Maurice Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Thompson "Maurice Thompson") in 1878, was the first book in English about hunting with a [bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting "Bowhunting") ever published.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witchery_of_Archery#cite_note-1) Its full title is _**The Witchery of Archery: A Complete Manual of Archery. With Many Chapters of Adventures by Field and Flood, and an Appendix Containing Practical Directions for the Manufacture and Use of Archery Implements**_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witchery_of_Archery#cite_note-2) It was the first important book about [archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery") written in English since _[Toxophilus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxophilus "Toxophilus")_, which was written in 1545.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witchery_of_Archery#cite_note-3) It was said that _Witchery_ "...has as much effect on archery as _[Uncle Tom's Cabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle\_Tom's\_Cabin "Uncle Tom's Cabin")_ had on the [Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witchery_of_Archery#cite_note-4)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Witchery_of_Archery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

When Thompson wrote _The Witchery of Archery_, he filled it with various stories, many of which were humorous. However, it also gave practical advice on the sport, such as the manufacturing of archery paraphernalia and how to use the equipment while hunting.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witchery_of_Archery#cite_note-5)

_The Witchery of Archery_ was accredited for returning the sport of archery to public interest. Some of this was due to rifles bringing back bad memories of the American Civil War.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witchery_of_Archery#cite_note-6) However, the revival also served some larger, pragmatic purpose: ex-Confederate soldiers were not allowed guns, but needed hunting to survive; archery became a convenient substitution. In addition, the late 1800s saw the last of the [American Indian Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Indian_Wars "American Indian Wars"), thus romanticizing the Native Americans and their cultures, which, in most accounts, included expert archery. In 1880, with the book less than two years old, [patents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent "Patent") relating to archery items greatly increased. More than any other book, _The Witchery of Archery_ led to the increased interest in archery for the next half-century.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witchery_of_Archery#cite_note-7)

A year after _The Witchery of Archery_ was published, Thompson was selected as the first president of the [National Archery Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archery_Association?action=edit&redlink=1 "National Archery Association (page does not exist)"), largely due to the book.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witchery_of_Archery#cite_note-8)

A writer of several books, Thompson seemed to show little pride in writing _The Witchery of Archery_. On the title pages of his various works, he would list several titles he authored, but never did he list '"_The Witchery of Archery'_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witchery_of_Archery#cite_note-9)

American hunter and physician

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9f/Dr._Saxton_Pope.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dr._Saxton_Pope.jpg)

Dr. Saxton Pope

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/29/Saxton_Pope_and_grizzly.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saxton_Pope_and_grizzly.jpg)

Picture of Pope taken while grizzly hunting at Yellowstone

**Saxton Temple Pope** (September 4, 1875 – August 8, 1926) was an American doctor, teacher, author and outdoorsman. He is most famous as the father of modern [bow hunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_hunting "Bow hunting"), and for his close relationship with [Ishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishi "Ishi"), the last member of the [Yahi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahi "Yahi") tribe and the last known [American Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") to be raised largely isolated from Western culture.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-bio-1)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saxton_Pope&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Born in [Fort Stockton, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Stockton,_Texas "Fort Stockton, Texas") as the son of an army surgeon, Pope grew up in military camps and frontier towns, where he learned outdoor skills and became an athlete. This is where he first learned archery, as well as horsemanship, riflery, knifemaking, and other skills. He built and attempted to fly a glider.

He later went to medical school at the [University of California, Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley") graduating in 1899. He set up a practice in [Watsonville, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watsonville,_California "Watsonville, California") near San Francisco, married Emma Wightman, a medical school classmate, and had four children. In 1912, he became a surgical instructor at the medical school.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-bio-1)

## Relationship with Ishi

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saxton_Pope&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Relationship with Ishi")]

The medical school where Pope taught was located near the [museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoebe_A._Hearst_Museum_of_Anthropology "Phoebe A. Hearst Museum of Anthropology") where Ishi worked as a janitor, having been brought there for study by Professor [T. T. Waterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._T._Waterman "T. T. Waterman") of the [University of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California "University of California") Department of Anthropology. Because Ishi had grown up in the isolated Yahi tribe, he had little immunity to diseases, and Pope met Ishi during his stays at the University hospital. Pope learned some of the Yahi language, and spent much time with Ishi, learning of his life and listening to the Yahi tribal folklore. Ishi taught Pope how to make bows and arrows as the Yahi did, and how to hunt with them. Pope and Ishi remained close until Ishi's death from [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis") in 1916.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-2) In spite of this close relationship and against Ishi's frequently stated wishes, Pope insisted that Ishi be autopsied after death and his brain removed.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-3)

## Later life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saxton_Pope&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life")]

Pope became an avid bowhunter during his time with Ishi, and he continued that after Ishi's death. In 1920, with special permission, Pope and a companion, Arthur Young, went hunting [grizzly bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grizzly_bear "Grizzly bear") in [Yellowstone National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_National_Park "Yellowstone National Park") with hand made bows and steel tipped arrows, taking several. The stuffed and mounted bears are on display at the California Academy of Sciences.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-bio-1) Pope later wrote a book, _Hunting with the Bow and Arrow_, which remains in print. He continued bowhunting until his death in 1926 from [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club#cite_note-bio-1)

**James Maurice Thompson** (September 9, 1844 – February 15, 1901) was an American novelist, poet, essayist, archer and naturalist.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Maurice_Thompson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

James Maurice Thompson was born in 1844 in the former town of Fairfield, Indiana, located in [Franklin County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_County,_Indiana "Franklin County, Indiana") to a Baptist minister and his wife. Near the end of the decade, the family moved to northern Georgia. He was educated by tutors in the classical languages, literature, French and mathematics; he used his mathematical training to advantage by becoming a [civil engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_engineer "Civil engineer").

During the [Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), Maurice Thompson and his brother [Will Henry Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Thompson_(archer) "William Thompson (archer)") (born 1848) fought as privates in the Confederate Army.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Thompson#cite_note-1)

After the war, Thompson took up residence in [Calhoun, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calhoun,_Georgia "Calhoun, Georgia"), where he studied surveying, engineering, and the law. He lived in Calhoun for two years, and began publishing the first of his articles while living there.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Thompson#cite_note-2)

In 1867 Thompson began a botanical and ornithological survey of [Lake Okeechobee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Okeechobee "Lake Okeechobee") in Florida. After finishing this work, Thompson and his brother moved to [Crawfordsville, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crawfordsville,_Indiana "Crawfordsville, Indiana"). Maurice began working as an engineer on a railroad being built in the area, and the Thompson brothers married sisters.

In 1871 the brothers opened a law office together. In 1873 Maurice resumed submitting articles for publication ([Atlantic Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic") published his first), after which he undertook a series of articles on [archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery"). He was published in _[New York Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Tribune "New York Tribune")_, _[Atlantic Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic\_Monthly "Atlantic Monthly")_, and _[Harper's Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper's\_Monthly "Harper's Monthly")_. His first book appeared in 1875 and over the ensuing years he wrote in different genres, including novels and poetry.

Thompson was elected to the Indiana State Legislature in 1879. His brother Will moved to [Seattle, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle,_Washington "Seattle, Washington") and became Western Counsel for the [Great Northern Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_Railway_(U.S.) "Great Northern Railway (U.S.)"), and remained active in Confederate affairs, as well as publishing a poem, "High Tide at Gettysburg". Thompson was the State Geologist of Indiana from 1885 to 1888.

## Writing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Maurice_Thompson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Writing")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/THOMPSON%281892%29_Poems.jpg/250px-THOMPSON%281892%29_Poems.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:THOMPSON(1892)_Poems.jpg)

Poems, 1892

Thompson became well known as a [local colorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_literary_regionalism "American literary regionalism"), with works ranging from local history to archery. His first book, _Hoosier Mosaics_, published in 1875, was a collection of short stories illustrating the people and atmosphere of small [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana") towns. He followed it with a successful compilation of his published essays, _[The Witchery of Archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Witchery\_of\_Archery "The Witchery of Archery")_, which was well received for its wit and use of common language. At this same time, Thompson also published several collections of naturalistic poetry, though they weren't well received at the time.

Thompson wrote the poem "To the South" that was reprinted in [George Washington Cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_Cable "George Washington Cable")'s influential and controversial essay, "The Freedmen's Case in Equity" in 1885. This poem expressed Thompson's reaction to the freeing of the slaves, and implied that some other Southerners were not as angry about the overturning of that institution as Northerners presumed.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Thompson#cite_note-3)[Rutherford B. Hayes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutherford_B._Hayes "Rutherford B. Hayes"), in 1892, read eight lines from Thompson's "An Address by an Ex-Confederate Soldier to the Grand Army of the Republic", calling him "the finest poet of the Confederacy".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Thompson#cite_note-4)

Through the 1880s, Thompson moved into the realm of fiction. His early works featured the common thread of simple southern life, taken mostly from Thompson's childhood. With his 1886 semi-autobiographical novel, _A Banker of Bankersville_, he returned to his [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana") roots. Arguably his most successful and well-known novel was _[Alice of Old Vincennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice\_of\_Old\_Vincennes "Alice of Old Vincennes")_. The novel vividly depicted Indiana during the [Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution").

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Maurice_Thompson&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Death")]

Thompson died shortly after publication of _Alice of Old Vincennes_, on February 15, 1901, of pneumonia, aged 56.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Thompson#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Thompson#cite_note-6)

Hunting by archery

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/171114-F-LS255-0011.JPG/330px-171114-F-LS255-0011.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:171114-F-LS255-0011.JPG)

**Bowhunting** (or **bow hunting**) is the practice of [hunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunting "Hunting")[game animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_(food) "Game (food)") by [archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery"). Many [indigenous peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples "Indigenous peoples") have employed the technique as their primary hunting method for thousands of years, and it has survived into contemporary use for sport and hunting.

## Modern history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Modern history")]

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/29/Saxton_Pope_and_grizzly.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saxton_Pope_and_grizzly.jpg)

Picture of Pope taken while [grizzly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grizzly_bear "Grizzly bear") hunting at [Yellowstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_National_Park "Yellowstone National Park")

The last of the [Yahi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahi#Yahi "Yahi") tribe, an indigenous man known as [Ishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishi "Ishi"), came out of hiding in California in 1911.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-2) His doctor, [Saxton Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxton_Pope "Saxton Pope"), learned many of Ishi's traditional archery skills, and popularized them.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-4) The [Pope and Young Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_and_Young_Club "Pope and Young Club"), founded in 1961 and named in honor of Pope and his friend, Arthur Young, became one of North America's leading bowhunting and conservation organizations. Founded as a nonprofit scientific organization, the club was patterned after the [Boone and Crockett Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boone_and_Crockett_Club "Boone and Crockett Club") and advocated responsible bowhunting by promoting quality, [fair chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_chase "Fair chase") hunting, and sound conservation practices. Modern game archery owes much of its success to [Fred Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Bear "Fred Bear"), an American bow hunter and bow manufacturer.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-Bertalan2007-5)

## Equipment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Equipment")]

[Arrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow "Arrow"), [bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_(weapon) "Bow (weapon)") and [sights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sights "Sights") are commonly of the more modern varieties. However, all effective variations, including [crossbows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossbow "Crossbow") and [wooden bows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self_bow "Self bow") launching wooden arrows with stone points, are used. [Arrowheads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrowhead "Arrowhead") are chosen to ensure lethality. Broadheads feature blades that jut out from the shaft at an angle to cause more damage to the target; some models have retractable blades that only deploy once they hit the target.

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Crossbow_Hunting.jpg/250px-Crossbow_Hunting.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crossbow_Hunting.jpg)

Hunting [crossbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossbow "Crossbow")

Big game hunting requires a draw weight of more than 35 [pounds-force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_(force) "Pound (force)") (16 [kilograms-force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilogram-force "Kilogram-force")). For larger game such as elk or moose, more than 50 lbf (23 kgf) is suggested. Most male American archers can draw a bow rated at 50–60 lbf (23–27 kgf), most women 30–40 lbf (14–18 kgf).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-6)

Lighter arrows, all else equal, will give a higher speed and a flatter trajectory.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-7) Arrows with greater mass carry more [momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momentum "Momentum"), and penetrate better in large animals; a minimum mass of 650 [grains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grain_(unit) "Grain (unit)") (40 [grams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram "Gram")) is recommended for animals such as deer, pigs, etc. and 900 gr (60 g) for the largest game.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-8)

## Methods of hunting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Methods of hunting")]

In contrast to a rifle hunter, who may shoot effectively from ranges in excess of 200 yards (180 m); archers usually restrict shots to 2.3 to 42 yards (2 to 38 m).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-9) The distance depends upon individual ability, the target animal, the bow strength, terrain, arrow and weather. The bow hunter may walk along the ground slowly, looking for game and stalking it carefully in the final approach. This type of slow, methodical stalking, is called "spot and stalk." Hunters often wear [camouflage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camouflage "Camouflage") clothing and walk upwind (with the wind in their face) so that game ahead of them cannot smell them.

In "stand hunting," the hunter waits for game to come to them, usually near food, water, or known trails. Brush and other natural materials may be placed for cover, or a "ground blind" that looks like a camouflage tent may be used.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-Woodrow-10) They usually "pop" up and can be set up from folded in a few minutes. The hunter may wait on a wooden or metal stand elevated in a tree, from three to six meters (3.5 to 6.5 yd).

Bowhunting for fish is called [bowfishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowfishing "Bowfishing"). Bowfishing equipment usually adds a line attached to a spool or a reel as well as a specially designed, heavier, barbed arrow. Most bow-fishers do not use sights, but if they do have sights they are different from standard ones to allow for [refraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refraction "Refraction").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-11)

## Legal and cultural considerations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Legal and cultural considerations")]

Bowhunting often has different seasons and restrictions from firearm hunting, and they differ significantly between areas. Legal and cultural approaches specific to the area must be taken into consideration by the hunter.

### Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Europe")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Bogenjagd_in_Europa.png/250px-Bogenjagd_in_Europa.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bogenjagd_in_Europa.png)

Legal status of bowhunting in Europe with countries allowing bowhunting in green

Nations including Denmark, France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Hungary, Finland and Bulgaria use bow and arrow hunting as a hunting tool in modern game management. Some European countries, including the United Kingdom, prohibit bowhunting.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-12) Bowhunting, like target archery, was revived in the UK during the Victorian era,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-13) but has been banned since 1965.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-14) Recently a law was passed in [Estonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonia "Estonia") that would allow bowhunting of [small game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_game "Small game").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-15)

### United States and Canada

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: United States and Canada")]

In the United States and Canada, as with other styles of hunting, bowhunting is regulated by individual provinces and states. Regulations often address issues such as which area to hunt in, what time of year (season), and which sex and species of game may be taken. In many cases, a special archery season is set aside, to minimize interference from rifle hunters. While bowhunting can run into rifle hunting seasons, hunter orange is typically required to be worn during the cross over seasons. In addition, in an effort to maximize game recovery and shot lethality, there are often technical regulations, such as a minimum draw weight, minimum width of head, and lack of barbs.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-16)

In general most bow hunting for big game begins in late August or early September in northern states and Canadian provinces, and slightly later in southern states.

### New Zealand

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: New Zealand")]

Organized bow hunting began in New Zealand in 1945. The New Zealand government regulates bowhunting.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-NZ_REG-17) An annual 3 day field shoot tournament is held every king's birthday weekend at various locations throughout New Zealand. Bowhunters must have permission to hunt on private land, and they cannot hunt in DOC lands, national parks, or any other reserves without a permit. All native species are protected; only introduced species are legal quarry.

There are no special seasons for bowhunters or for hunting with a firearm.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-NZ_DOC-18) There is an active bow hunters' society.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-NZ_BS-19)

### Australia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Australia")]

Bowhunting is practiced in Australia and is not specifically subject to regulation by law. Only non-native species are recognized as game by the Australian Bowhunters Association. However, native species may be killed during government-authorized culls.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-20)

The states of [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_(Australia) "Victoria (Australia)") and [New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales "New South Wales") both regulate bowhunting. In Victoria hunting is regulated through the Department of Sustainability and Environment (DSE).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-VIC_DSE-21) In New South Wales this is done through the Department of Primary Industry.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-NSW_GC-22) At the current time there are no specific hunting regulations in other states and territories.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-ABA-23)

In July 2013 the New South Wales Government disbanded the Game Council, and temporarily suspended licensed hunting in NSW State forests.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-NSW_ABO_GC-24)

While both Victoria and New South Wales place licensing requirements on would-be bowhunters, the sport is self-regulated. The Australian Bowhunters Association and local clubs assess hunters through the Bowhunter Proficiency Certificate (BPC) which is designed to ensure that animals are killed according to humane principles.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-BPC-25)

### Zimbabwe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Zimbabwe")]

Zimbabwe has legally permitted hunting with compound bows since 1989 as an exception, and since 1999 under formal legislation. Minimum arrow weights and bow draws are mandated. Bowhunting is only allowed on private or tribal lands, but not in national parks. Bowhunters must be accompanied by licensed guides or professional hunters.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-26) Bowhunting of elephants is mostly conducted in Zimbabwe.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-27) Following international outrage over the [killing of Cecil the lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Cecil_the_lion "Killing of Cecil the lion") in 2015, the Parks and Wildlife Management Authority banned all bowhunting unless specifically authorized as well as other hunting restrictions.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-28)

## Opposition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Opposition")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Newport20230330.jpg/250px-Newport20230330.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Newport20230330.jpg)

Duck in [Newport Beach, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Beach,_California "Newport Beach, California") injured by arrow

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/CDOW20101109.jpg/250px-CDOW20101109.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CDOW20101109.jpg)

Duck injured by crossbow arrows in [Colorado Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Springs,_Colorado "Colorado Springs, Colorado")

Some are deeply opposed to bow hunting in particular, on the grounds of cruelty. The organization [People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_for_the_Ethical_Treatment_of_Animals "People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals") states that "quick kills are rare, and many animals suffer prolonged, painful deaths when hunters severely injure but fail to kill them."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-29)

### Wounding rates

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bowhunting&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Wounding rates")]

A study conducted by the [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma") Fish and Wildlife Agencies found that approximately 50% of deer that were shot were never recovered, noting that this rate was similar to data from other studies. Some deer survived for up to 5–7 days before succumbing to their wounds. "71% to 82% of all shots taken" miss the target[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-30) and "shot placement is, for all practical purposes, random".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-31)

In another study from [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"), archers who had passed a pre-season accuracy test claimed that 82% of deer hit were recovered within 24 hours.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-32)

Danish licensed bowhunters are required to complete a report every time that they kill a [roe deer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe_deer "Roe deer"). (To become a licensed bowhunter in [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") it is necessary to pass a very demanding proficiency test, including a test of accuracy in which five of six arrows must hit within the vital area of game targets ranging from roe deer to pheasant in size at unknown distances up to 25 meters (27 yd). Only 2% of Danish bowhunters use traditional equipment.) For 1999–2004, these reports showed that 576 arrows were released at roe deer. 92.5% of these shots resulted in a dead roe deer being collected by the hunter, and 2.6% are documented as misses. In 5% of reports the deer was hit and wounded (as indicated by bodily fluids on the ground or on the arrow), but not recovered by the hunter. The European Bowhunters Association states that "this percentage compares favorably with other means of harvesting roe deer in Europe."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowhunting#cite_note-33)
