# M. R. James # 1940 - **Class of 2003** **_Bowhunter, Contributor to the Sport, Influence on the Sport_** M. R. James spent 35 memorable years writing and editing material for _Bowhunter_ magazine, the publication that he founded in 1971. Under his editorial direction, _Bowhunter_ evolved into the most successful special-interest periodical in archery history. ![Image 2](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/MRJ%20Pics%20002.JPG-1.jpg)M.R. is a living legend in bowhunting circles, and is still living his lifetime of bowhunting experiences. Leading by example, he has made vast contributions to the education of bow hunters through his writings and through encouraging others to share their experiences in the written form. Born under the zodiacal sign of "The Archer" in Wabash County, Illinois in 1940, M.R. traces his interest in archery to when he crafted his first crude bows and arrows from native saplings while still in grade school, and by the age of 12 had saved enough money from farm work and household chores to buy his first "real" longbow and arrows. While a college student, he began to write and sell short stories and articles to national magazines. His writing career was nurtured by another Hall of Famer,[Roy Hoff](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/Hoff%20Roy.html), the ![Image 3](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/mrhead.jpg)editor of Archery Magazine. His byline then began to appear in the nations leading archery and outdoor publications. His biography is listed regularly in Who's Who in the West, Who's Who in America and Who's Who in the World. Today M.R. James continues to pursue this dual passions, writing and bowhunting. He tirelessly promotes the sport while traveling extensively, serving as an informed and eloquent public relations emissary for the entire North American bowhunting community. ![Image 4](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/1stblbear1971.jpg-1.jpg)![Image 5](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/1971%20anteloope%20hunt%20in%20Nebgraska,%20black%20window%20remains%20altime%20hunting%20bow.jpg-1.jpg) 1971 - Far left photo is M. R.'s first Colorado Black Bear taken with bow. Other photo is of Mule Deer taken also in 1971 in Nebraska. # Notes of Interest![Image 6](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/Dave%20&%20MR.jpg) * Editor/Founder of _Bowhunter_ Magazine, 1971 thru 2006 * Editor of First Pope and Young Club Record Book, 1975; P&Y Board Member for More Than 20 Years; P&Y President, 2006 thru 2010; AHOF President, 2009, ’10, ’11, ‘12 * National Bowhunter Education Foundation Board Member, 1979-‘92 * Award-Winning Author, Magazine Feature Writer, Columnist, Contributor, and Public Speaker; Professional Bowhunters Society Life Member * Recipient of Outdoor Writers Association of America’s “Excellence in Craft” Lifetime Achievement Award, 1999 * Successfully Bowhunted 35 States and 7 Canadian Provinces, Collecting 21 Separate Species of North American Big Game * Received t he Dave Staples Golden Arrow Award 2019![Image 7](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/mrjames.jpg) ![Image 8](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/MRJ%20Pics%20001.JPG-1.jpg) ![Image 9](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/MR%20corrrect.jpg) ![Image 10](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/AHF01315-1.JPG) ![Image 11](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/img325.jpg) M.R. and wife Janet ![Image 12](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/New%20Image.JPG) ![Image 13](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/JAMES/AHF01319-1-1.JPG)

# USA Archery News

### May 31, 2018

# USA Archery Celebrates the Life of Hardy Ward

Earlier this month, National and World Champion Hardy Ward passed away. He will be greatly missed by all who knew him, especially his archery family.

Ward, born in Texas in 1949, represented the U.S. at the 1967 and 1969 World Championships after winning his first National Champion title at age 16 in 1966. At his World Championship debut, Ward won individual bronze and team gold. In '69, Ward shot the world's first 1220 FITA and took individual and team gold.

That same year, [Sports Illustrated](https://www.si.com/vault/1969/08/11/610524/the-hardy-boy-and-his-bow-and-arrow) created a beautiful profile on the talented young archer, saying: "Hardy Ward shoots with some of the crookedest fingers and straightest arrows in the world of archery."

Hardy first picked up archer at age 5 when his parents bought him a $6 bow for his birthday. Until age 12, he only practiced in his backyard, shooting milk cartons and small animals in local fields. His father recalled to SI: "'We didn't have any idea how good he was, so we all piled into the car and took him to a tournament in Arkansas to find out.'" Ward shot a new national record and quickly joined the competition circuit.

Earl Hoyt had recalled Ward was the first archer to win a national title with a clicker on his bow. He was always ahead of the game in archery technology. He was a pioneer in creating materials for the tennis and archery industries. At one time, his company "Waco" produced the majority of all archery metal products used globally, including products for Easton and Bemen.

When modern archery was added back to the Olympic program in 1972, Ward missed making the U.S. team following injuries before and during the Trials. Ward was part of the Army's gifted athlete training program along with his teammates who went on to compete at the Games - Ed Eliason and John Williams.

Ward eventually got into coaching archery and developing revolutionary coaching methodology. He dedicated so much of his life to growing archery at the grassroots level and developing incredible archers that shared his passion for the sport.

One of Ward's best friends, Skip Trafford, commented: "Hardy Ward was without a doubt America's most talented _all round_ archer. His experience touched on every point of the archery compass. He reminds me of the proverbial blind men and the elephant. He had Jay's turn-on-a-dime switch from humor to the X zone, Ed's never-say-die competitiveness, Darrel's no nonsense focus on success, Earl's bowyer & engineering knowledge, Rob's business savvy, Ann's determination, Vic's competitive longevity, Dick's coaching eye, Tom's float all boats determination and Don's attention to detail.

"Hardy was my dear friend of almost 50 years. He was not only my Best Man but my son's namesake. He was an Eagle Scout, a proud member of our nation's honor guard in Arlington Cemetery and a devout patriot.I was in touch with Hardy right up to the final hours of his passing. My family and I loved him like the brother and godfather he was to my wife and I and our four kids. The global archery community lost a huge pioneer with his passing."

# USA Archery News

### May 31, 2018

# USA Archery Celebrates the Life of Hardy Ward

Earlier this month, National and World Champion Hardy Ward passed away. He will be greatly missed by all who knew him, especially his archery family.

Ward, born in Texas in 1949, represented the U.S. at the 1967 and 1969 World Championships after winning his first National Champion title at age 16 in 1966. At his World Championship debut, Ward won individual bronze and team gold. In '69, Ward shot the world's first 1220 FITA and took individual and team gold.

That same year, [Sports Illustrated](https://www.si.com/vault/1969/08/11/610524/the-hardy-boy-and-his-bow-and-arrow) created a beautiful profile on the talented young archer, saying: "Hardy Ward shoots with some of the crookedest fingers and straightest arrows in the world of archery."

Hardy first picked up archer at age 5 when his parents bought him a $6 bow for his birthday. Until age 12, he only practiced in his backyard, shooting milk cartons and small animals in local fields. His father recalled to SI: "'We didn't have any idea how good he was, so we all piled into the car and took him to a tournament in Arkansas to find out.'" Ward shot a new national record and quickly joined the competition circuit.

Earl Hoyt had recalled Ward was the first archer to win a national title with a clicker on his bow. He was always ahead of the game in archery technology. He was a pioneer in creating materials for the tennis and archery industries. At one time, his company "Waco" produced the majority of all archery metal products used globally, including products for Easton and Bemen.

When modern archery was added back to the Olympic program in 1972, Ward missed making the U.S. team following injuries before and during the Trials. Ward was part of the Army's gifted athlete training program along with his teammates who went on to compete at the Games - Ed Eliason and John Williams.

Ward eventually got into coaching archery and developing revolutionary coaching methodology. He dedicated so much of his life to growing archery at the grassroots level and developing incredible archers that shared his passion for the sport.

One of Ward's best friends, Skip Trafford, commented: "Hardy Ward was without a doubt America's most talented _all round_ archer. His experience touched on every point of the archery compass. He reminds me of the proverbial blind men and the elephant. He had Jay's turn-on-a-dime switch from humor to the X zone, Ed's never-say-die competitiveness, Darrel's no nonsense focus on success, Earl's bowyer & engineering knowledge, Rob's business savvy, Ann's determination, Vic's competitive longevity, Dick's coaching eye, Tom's float all boats determination and Don's attention to detail.

"Hardy was my dear friend of almost 50 years. He was not only my Best Man but my son's namesake. He was an Eagle Scout, a proud member of our nation's honor guard in Arlington Cemetery and a devout patriot.I was in touch with Hardy right up to the final hours of his passing. My family and I loved him like the brother and godfather he was to my wife and I and our four kids. The global archery community lost a huge pioneer with his passing."

# Tag Archives: archery history

 August 22, 2023 · 10:54 am 

## [Book Review—The Secrets of Modern Archery](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/2023/08/22/book-review-the-secrets-of-modern-archery/)

![Image 2](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/cover-of-the-secrets-of-ma.jpg?w=225&h=300)The title of this book was intriguing, very intriguing, so I bought it. With such a title one might expect hundreds of secrets to be revealed, and if not hundreds, then many dozens, or certainly a few handfuls, or at least a handful. What I found was zero secrets: zero, nada, zilch, none. Which didn’t surprise me because as I have often expressed the thought that “there are no secrets in archery.”

The kindest interpretation I can put on the use of the word “Secrets” in the title is bait and switch. Actually I only bought the book because the author, Jake Veit, is not a lightweight, but he should know better.

Here is the table of contents:

Ch 1 The Secrets of Modern Archery (where did we come from in the U.S.)  
 Ch 2 Olympic Games  
 Ch 3 Interest in Bowhunting in the U.S.  
 Ch 4 Promoters that (sic) helped archery grow (Manufacturers, Bowhunters, and Competitors)  
 Ch 5 Individuals (sic) Patent of Archery over time  
 Ch 6 After World War II  
 Ch 7 Shooting Archery for Money  
 Ch 8 Compound Bow When?  
 Ch 9 NFAA (continued)  
 Ch 10 NAA Continued  
 Ch 11 An NFAA Instructor Certification Program (from the 1980’s with test)  
 Ch 12 Archery in General Today.  
 Followed by a huge glossary of terms.

It is clear that the book suffers from the lack of the services of a good copy editor/proofreader. Some chapters (4 and 8) are about one page long. The glossary is 67 pages. The chapter titles have, shall we say, unusual capitalizations. Other problems in titles are in Chapter 4 it should be “Promoters Who . . . “ not “Promoters that . . . “; in Chapter 5 I assume “Individuals Patent . . . “ should be “Individual Patents. . . . “ The title to Chapter 8 is mysterious; just what is the topic? The titles to Chapters 9 (NFAA (continued)) and 10 (NAA Continued) aren’t parallel and should be. There is a subtitle “Summery to Today” in Chapter 10 which I supposed was to be “Summary Up Until Now.” But proofreading is a bitch. I don’t know how many things I have missed editing copy and proofing it, but it is not a small number of things.

The author was kind enough to list all of his sources, all of which I have read, so if you have not, you may find some of this interesting, reports on the annual meetings of the NAA aside, I assume.

Whether you might benefit from reading this book is debatable. There is little to help a coach to coach better, and nothing to help and archer shoot better, but there is a great deal of background information, much of it political in nature. (If you don’t think archery is political, work with USA Archery for a while and then report back to me.)

Oh, there are no secrets in the book, if you were wondering.

**The Secrets of Modern Archery**  
 by Jake Veit

## [Hugh D.H. Soar(1926–2022)](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/2022/11/19/hugh-d-h-soar-1926-2022/)

I just got notified that Hugh Soar has died, which was not unexpected as he was closer to being 100 than 90, but still sad. While one could declare that Hugh was a big fish in a small pond, he was the pre-eminent archery historian of the Western Tradition in the world, in my opinion.

He wrote a slew of books on archery history, all written in what I call a charming, somewhat archaic, style. I had the honor of editing his last book, [The Young at Archery](https://www.amazon.com/Young-Archery-Hugh-D-H-Soar/dp/0991332679/ref=sr_1_4?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-4). Other titles included:

[Straight and True: A Select History of the Arrow](https://www.amazon.com/Straight-True-Select-History-Arrow-ebook/dp/B009PQM7F6/ref=sr_1_1?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-1)

[The Crooked Stick: A History of the Longbow](https://www.amazon.com/Crooked-Stick-History-Longbow-ebook/dp/B00492CFXA/ref=sr_1_2?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-2)

[The Romance of Archery: A Social History of the Longbow](https://www.amazon.com/Romance-Archery-Social-History-Longbow/dp/1594160678/ref=sr_1_3?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-3)

[Secrets of the English War Bow](https://www.amazon.com/Secrets-English-War-Hugh-Soar/dp/1594161267/ref=sr_1_7?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-7)

[How to Shoot the Longbow: A Guide from Historical and Applied Sources](https://www.amazon.com/How-Shoot-Longbow-Historical-Applied-ebook/dp/B085J1VQT3/ref=sr_1_8?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-8)

[Of Bowmen and Battles](https://www.amazon.com/Bowmen-Battles-Hugh-David-Hewitt/dp/0951764519/ref=sr_1_1?crid=1B5SB8W79HD8Z&keywords=Of+Bowmen+and+Battles&qid=1668871790&s=books&sprefix=of+bowmen+and+battles%2Cstripbooks%2C92&sr=1-1)

Hugh was sought out for his expertise by television shows and other media, and his collection of more than 240 bows and other artifacts is among the finest in the world.

Hugh was a member of the Mary Rose Trust Committee. The Trust’s primary aims are to preserve, display and spread knowledge about the 16 th century warship, [Mary Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Rose), which sank in the Solent on 19 July 1545 and was salvaged by the Trust in October 1982. The sixteenth century in England was right in Hugh’s wheelhouse, and the ship contained many, many bow staves and bows and arrow shafts, broadheads, etc.

He received a number of honors in his life and he was a member of quite a few historical archery companies, such as the British Longbow Society, the Royal Toxophilite Society, of which he was General Secretary for eleven years, and he founded the Craft Guild of Traditional Bowyers and Fletchers.

He is survived by his wife, Veronica-Mae, whose writings also graced the pages of _Archery Focus_ magazine, and several children and grandchildren.

I am honored to have gotten to work with him.

## [Archery in the News!](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/2022/04/17/archery-in-the-news/)

An article in _The Guardian_ newspaper pointed to archeological discoveries which could substantially push back the date archery was used for hunting in Europe. According to that article:

> “Early archers would have been able to kill their prey at a considerable distance while at the same time giving their diets a protein boost without endangering themselves, say researchers. It has also become clear that bow-and-arrow technology is ancient, with some of the oldest arrowheads traced to caves in South Africa and dated to around 64,000 years ago.
> 
> 
> “Outside Africa, the earliest evidence of archery was some 48,000-year-old arrowheads found in a Sri Lankan cave two years ago. However, that date is now expected to be pushed back to around 54,000 years . . .”

Of course, this doesn’t mean that researchers or reporters have any idea what primitive archery was like. The article went on:

> “An animal 100 metres away will think you are too distant to be dangerous and won’t move away,” Slimak told the Observer. ‘With a bow and arrow, you could pick it off easily. Equally importantly, you’ll be too far away for it to attack you if it is wounded and gets angry. So you can hunt safely and provide more protein for your group.’”

A one hundred meter (109 yard) shot? With primitive bows and primitive arrows? Pick it off easily? Egad! And not just “primitive” bows and arrows, but some of the first ever made in Europe!

## [Did the Ancient Greeks Really Think Archers Were Cowards?](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/2020/05/19/did-the-ancient-greeks-really-think-archers-were-cowards/)

One of my favorite bloggers is Spenser Alexander McDaniel, who is a young man still in college studying classics. He blogs about things historical and this post caught my eye. I recommend it ([Did the Ancient Greeks Really Think Archers Were Cowards?](https://talesoftimesforgotten.com/2020/05/18/did-the-ancient-greeks-really-think-archers-were-cowards/)) to you if you are interested and his blog also.

He writes very, very well for one so young. He does quite a bit of debunking of the stories we tell ourselves about ancient peoples and the more I read his posts, the more “just like us” these people become. Granted they had quite different beliefs and attitudes, but otherwise the ancient Greeks, Romans, Persians, Hebrews, etc. would fit into our modern spectrum of peoples quite easily.

I am currently reading a 1643 treatise on archery, written by a Chinese expert, and it sounds quite modern (not so surprisingly as the bows will teach us what we need to know).

I am fascinated by fact that they used quite heavy bows, but of course these were a military weapons, not just a target toys. Once they developed good form they would begin exercising to build up their ability to draw heavier drawing bows. Some of their practice bows went over 200# of draw! These were bows that were designed not to be shot, just to train with, but there were occasionally bows with such draw weights that were designed to be shot. Just thinking about that causes me to ache!

So, do you know any exercises designed to be able to increase the amount of draw weight you can handle? If so, I would like to know about them.

_Steve_

PS I will be writing a review of this book for _Archery Focus_ magazine as soon as I get it done. Interestingly the author was shooting off of the point 200 years before Horace Ford popularized that practice in the western tradition. I think westerners could learn a few things by looking at Asian traditions.

## [Book Review—The Secrets of Modern Archery](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/2023/08/22/book-review-the-secrets-of-modern-archery/)

![Image 2](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/cover-of-the-secrets-of-ma.jpg?w=225&h=300)The title of this book was intriguing, very intriguing, so I bought it. With such a title one might expect hundreds of secrets to be revealed, and if not hundreds, then many dozens, or certainly a few handfuls, or at least a handful. What I found was zero secrets: zero, nada, zilch, none. Which didn’t surprise me because as I have often expressed the thought that “there are no secrets in archery.”

The kindest interpretation I can put on the use of the word “Secrets” in the title is bait and switch. Actually I only bought the book because the author, Jake Veit, is not a lightweight, but he should know better.

Here is the table of contents:

Ch 1 The Secrets of Modern Archery (where did we come from in the U.S.)  
 Ch 2 Olympic Games  
 Ch 3 Interest in Bowhunting in the U.S.  
 Ch 4 Promoters that (sic) helped archery grow (Manufacturers, Bowhunters, and Competitors)  
 Ch 5 Individuals (sic) Patent of Archery over time  
 Ch 6 After World War II  
 Ch 7 Shooting Archery for Money  
 Ch 8 Compound Bow When?  
 Ch 9 NFAA (continued)  
 Ch 10 NAA Continued  
 Ch 11 An NFAA Instructor Certification Program (from the 1980’s with test)  
 Ch 12 Archery in General Today.  
 Followed by a huge glossary of terms.

It is clear that the book suffers from the lack of the services of a good copy editor/proofreader. Some chapters (4 and 8) are about one page long. The glossary is 67 pages. The chapter titles have, shall we say, unusual capitalizations. Other problems in titles are in Chapter 4 it should be “Promoters Who . . . “ not “Promoters that . . . “; in Chapter 5 I assume “Individuals Patent . . . “ should be “Individual Patents. . . . “ The title to Chapter 8 is mysterious; just what is the topic? The titles to Chapters 9 (NFAA (continued)) and 10 (NAA Continued) aren’t parallel and should be. There is a subtitle “Summery to Today” in Chapter 10 which I supposed was to be “Summary Up Until Now.” But proofreading is a bitch. I don’t know how many things I have missed editing copy and proofing it, but it is not a small number of things.

The author was kind enough to list all of his sources, all of which I have read, so if you have not, you may find some of this interesting, reports on the annual meetings of the NAA aside, I assume.

Whether you might benefit from reading this book is debatable. There is little to help a coach to coach better, and nothing to help and archer shoot better, but there is a great deal of background information, much of it political in nature. (If you don’t think archery is political, work with USA Archery for a while and then report back to me.)

Oh, there are no secrets in the book, if you were wondering.

**The Secrets of Modern Archery**  
 by Jake Veit  
 Published January 31, 2021  
 221 pages (soft cover) Amazon says 314 pages for some reason

Amazon Pricing (as of 8-22-23) PB $16.99, Kindle $3.99  
 MSLP $??? (Couldn’t find.)

## [Hugh D.H. Soar(1926–2022)](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/2022/11/19/hugh-d-h-soar-1926-2022/)

I just got notified that Hugh Soar has died, which was not unexpected as he was closer to being 100 than 90, but still sad. While one could declare that Hugh was a big fish in a small pond, he was the pre-eminent archery historian of the Western Tradition in the world, in my opinion.

He wrote a slew of books on archery history, all written in what I call a charming, somewhat archaic, style. I had the honor of editing his last book, [The Young at Archery](https://www.amazon.com/Young-Archery-Hugh-D-H-Soar/dp/0991332679/ref=sr_1_4?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-4). Other titles included:

[Straight and True: A Select History of the Arrow](https://www.amazon.com/Straight-True-Select-History-Arrow-ebook/dp/B009PQM7F6/ref=sr_1_1?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-1)

[The Crooked Stick: A History of the Longbow](https://www.amazon.com/Crooked-Stick-History-Longbow-ebook/dp/B00492CFXA/ref=sr_1_2?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-2)

[The Romance of Archery: A Social History of the Longbow](https://www.amazon.com/Romance-Archery-Social-History-Longbow/dp/1594160678/ref=sr_1_3?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-3)

[Secrets of the English War Bow](https://www.amazon.com/Secrets-English-War-Hugh-Soar/dp/1594161267/ref=sr_1_7?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-7)

[How to Shoot the Longbow: A Guide from Historical and Applied Sources](https://www.amazon.com/How-Shoot-Longbow-Historical-Applied-ebook/dp/B085J1VQT3/ref=sr_1_8?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-8)

[Of Bowmen and Battles](https://www.amazon.com/Bowmen-Battles-Hugh-David-Hewitt/dp/0951764519/ref=sr_1_1?crid=1B5SB8W79HD8Z&keywords=Of+Bowmen+and+Battles&qid=1668871790&s=books&sprefix=of+bowmen+and+battles%2Cstripbooks%2C92&sr=1-1)

Hugh was sought out for his expertise by television shows and other media, and his collection of more than 240 bows and other artifacts is among the finest in the world.

Hugh was a member of the Mary Rose Trust Committee. The Trust’s primary aims are to preserve, display and spread knowledge about the 16 th century warship, [Mary Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Rose), which sank in the Solent on 19 July 1545 and was salvaged by the Trust in October 1982. The sixteenth century in England was right in Hugh’s wheelhouse, and the ship contained many, many bow staves and bows and arrow shafts, broadheads, etc.

He received a number of honors in his life and he was a member of quite a few historical archery companies, such as the British Longbow Society, the Royal Toxophilite Society, of which he was General Secretary for eleven years, and he founded the Craft Guild of Traditional Bowyers and Fletchers.

He is survived by his wife, Veronica-Mae, whose writings also graced the pages of _Archery Focus_ magazine, and several children and grandchildren.

I am honored to have gotten to work with him.

## [Archery in the News!](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/2022/04/17/archery-in-the-news/)

An article in _The Guardian_ newspaper pointed to archeological discoveries which could substantially push back the date archery was used for hunting in Europe. According to that article:

> “Early archers would have been able to kill their prey at a considerable distance while at the same time giving their diets a protein boost without endangering themselves, say researchers. It has also become clear that bow-and-arrow technology is ancient, with some of the oldest arrowheads traced to caves in South Africa and dated to around 64,000 years ago.
> 
> 
> “Outside Africa, the earliest evidence of archery was some 48,000-year-old arrowheads found in a Sri Lankan cave two years ago. However, that date is now expected to be pushed back to around 54,000 years . . .”

Of course, this doesn’t mean that researchers or reporters have any idea what primitive archery was like. The article went on:

> “An animal 100 metres away will think you are too distant to be dangerous and won’t move away,” Slimak told the Observer. ‘With a bow and arrow, you could pick it off easily. Equally importantly, you’ll be too far away for it to attack you if it is wounded and gets angry. So you can hunt safely and provide more protein for your group.’”

A one hundred meter (109 yard) shot? With primitive bows and primitive arrows? Pick it off easily? Egad! And not just “primitive” bows and arrows, but some of the first ever made in Europe!

## [Did the Ancient Greeks Really Think Archers Were Cowards?](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/2020/05/19/did-the-ancient-greeks-really-think-archers-were-cowards/)

One of my favorite bloggers is Spenser Alexander McDaniel, who is a young man still in college studying classics. He blogs about things historical and this post caught my eye. I recommend it ([Did the Ancient Greeks Really Think Archers Were Cowards?](https://talesoftimesforgotten.com/2020/05/18/did-the-ancient-greeks-really-think-archers-were-cowards/)) to you if you are interested and his blog also.

He writes very, very well for one so young. He does quite a bit of debunking of the stories we tell ourselves about ancient peoples and the more I read his posts, the more “just like us” these people become. Granted they had quite different beliefs and attitudes, but otherwise the ancient Greeks, Romans, Persians, Hebrews, etc. would fit into our modern spectrum of peoples quite easily.

I am currently reading a 1643 treatise on archery, written by a Chinese expert, and it sounds quite modern (not so surprisingly as the bows will teach us what we need to know).

I am fascinated by fact that they used quite heavy bows, but of course these were a military weapons, not just a target toys. Once they developed good form they would begin exercising to build up their ability to draw heavier drawing bows. Some of their practice bows went over 200# of draw! These were bows that were designed not to be shot, just to train with, but there were occasionally bows with such draw weights that were designed to be shot. Just thinking about that causes me to ache!

So, do you know any exercises designed to be able to increase the amount of draw weight you can handle? If so, I would like to know about them.

_Steve_

PS I will be writing a review of this book for _Archery Focus_ magazine as soon as I get it done. Interestingly the author was shooting off of the point 200 years before Horace Ford popularized that practice in the western tradition. I think westerners could learn a few things by looking at Asian traditions.

# Roy Hoff (1903-1985)**** **Class of 1978 _![Image 2](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/Hoff/Hoff%20Camera-web.JPG)_** **_Bowhunter, Competitor_**Born in 1903, in Gunnison, Colorado, Roy owned, edited and published Archery magazine, the official publication of the National Field Archery Association for over 20 years. Through this publication, archery and bowhunting received national and international recognition. ![Image 3](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/Hoff/Hoff,%20typwriter-web.JPG)Hoff has contributed so much time and effort promoting archery in California that in 1962 the state organization, then known as the California Bowmen Hunters and Field Archery Association, gave special recognition to Roy by calling him the "Father of Organized Archery" in California. In 1962 he was awarded the NFAA "Compton Medal of Honor". Whether it be organized archery, bowhunting or tournament archery Roy was there-not for just a period of years, but from the start in 1943.![Image 4](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/Hoff/Roy%20Hoff3%20copy.jpg-1.jpg)**_![Image 5](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/Roy%20Hoff%208.jpg-1.jpg)_** 1972 Roy and Frieda Hoff relax in Hawaii # Notes of Interest * Founder of _Archery Magazine_, Official Publication of the National Field Archery Association * Champion Tournament Archer and Avid Bowhunter, Led the Fight for Archery-Only Hunting Seasons in the Early 1940s * First President of the California Bowmen Hunters, 1943. CBH State Target Champion, 1945 * Extensively Involved in the Formation and Growth of the NFAA * Tireless Promoter of Archery and Bowhunting for More Than 40 Years * Awarded the NFAA Compton Medal of Honor, 1962 ![Image 6](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/Hoff/Roy%20Hoff%20-%20Rhode%20Book%20pg%20141-1.jpg)![Image 7](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/Hoff/Roy%20Hoff4copy.jpg-1.JPG-1.jpg) ![Image 8](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/Hoff/hoff.jpg) ![Image 9](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/Hoff/Picture6.jpg) ![Image 10](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/Hoff/Archery%20-%2019.jpg) Karl Palmatier with Roy ![Image 11](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/images/Hoff/IMG_1617-web.JPG)

# USA Archery News

### September 28, 2026

# Yankton again the setting, though this time for the World Archery 3D Championships

![Image 4](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/280926115449-Cody%20Hasson%20World%203D%202026.jpg)

YANKTON, S.D. – Just as the last arrows were landing at the World Archery Field Championships in Yankton, the first of the archers were arriving for the World Archery 3D Championships.

Official practice takes place on Monday before competition begins on Tuesday morning. The 2026 World Archery 3D Championships run through until Saturday and the USA has a tournament-high 24 archers competing. Team trials for the U.S. were held in Yankton in early June.

In all, there are 246 archers from 24 countries taking part. The USA team includes Shiloh Butts, a team medalist in both 2022 and 2024. Jayme Buchanan and Julie Jones also return. Buchanan won bronze in two team events and Jones the one when the competition was held in Mokrice, Slovenia two years ago.

There will be a number of archers staying on from the World Archery Field Championships. Among them is history-maker Erin Hollom. Hollom was part of the trio, that also included Casey Kaufhold and Paige Pearce, to be the first to win women’s team gold for the USA at the World Field Championships.

As well as Hollom, others extending their stay in Yankton are Chloe Crandall, Grady Kane and Ava Jones. Crandall and Kane won multiple medals over the weekend at the World Field Championships. Crandall, Kane and Jones are just a few of the teenage talent making their World 3D debut. Others include Jewell Blakey and Gracelyn Sinclair.

Joella Bates will be making her fifth appearance at the World Archery 3D Championships, while Stephanie Correa will be featuring at a third World 3D. Michael Davenport, Cody Hasson (pictured above), Jeremiah Jones and Julie Jones all return, having made their debut in Slovenia two years ago. Others with previous World 3D experience include Jon Starks, Kim Timberlake and James Todd.

There will be a husband-and-wife pairing sporting the colors of the USA, with Julie Jones joined by husband Daniel in the traditional division.

_Lancaster Archery Foundation is kindly offering a $500 stipend to those who qualified for the World Archery 3D Championships._

You can follow the scores from Yankton[HERE](https://info.ianseo.net/26WA3DC/).

# Yankton again the setting, though this time for the World Archery 3D Championships

![Image 4](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/280926115449-Cody%20Hasson%20World%203D%202026.jpg)

YANKTON, S.D. – Just as the last arrows were landing at the World Archery Field Championships in Yankton, the first of the archers were arriving for the World Archery 3D Championships.

Official practice takes place on Monday before competition begins on Tuesday morning. The 2026 World Archery 3D Championships run through until Saturday and the USA has a tournament-high 24 archers competing. Team trials for the U.S. were held in Yankton in early June.

In all, there are 246 archers from 24 countries taking part. The USA team includes Shiloh Butts, a team medalist in both 2022 and 2024. Jayme Buchanan and Julie Jones also return. Buchanan won bronze in two team events and Jones the one when the competition was held in Mokrice, Slovenia two years ago.

There will be a number of archers staying on from the World Archery Field Championships. Among them is history-maker Erin Hollom. Hollom was part of the trio, that also included Casey Kaufhold and Paige Pearce, to be the first to win women’s team gold for the USA at the World Field Championships.

As well as Hollom, others extending their stay in Yankton are Chloe Crandall, Grady Kane and Ava Jones. Crandall and Kane won multiple medals over the weekend at the World Field Championships. Crandall, Kane and Jones are just a few of the teenage talent making their World 3D debut. Others include Jewell Blakey and Gracelyn Sinclair.

Joella Bates will be making her fifth appearance at the World Archery 3D Championships, while Stephanie Correa will be featuring at a third World 3D. Michael Davenport, Cody Hasson (pictured above), Jeremiah Jones and Julie Jones all return, having made their debut in Slovenia two years ago. Others with previous World 3D experience include Jon Starks, Kim Timberlake and James Todd.

There will be a husband-and-wife pairing sporting the colors of the USA, with Julie Jones joined by husband Daniel in the traditional division.

_Lancaster Archery Foundation is kindly offering a $500 stipend to those who qualified for the World Archery 3D Championships._

You can follow the scores from Yankton[HERE](https://info.ianseo.net/26WA3DC/).

### September 14, 2026

# Ten years on, Andre Shelby reflects on historic Rio gold and a lasting archery legacy

**![Image 4](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/110926110849-Andre%20Shelby%202016%20podium%20in%20Rio.jpg)Andre Shelby became Paralympic champion at the Rio Games on September 14, 2016. Ten years on, the moment remains difficult for him to fully comprehend.**

“Actually, about a month ago I just looked at all the matches that I shot in Rio and it’s still hard to believe,” Shelby said.

Shelby’s journey to the Paralympic podium had taken him through a long competition day in Rio, beginning around 7 a.m. and continuing until his final match late that evening.

“My last match was like eight, nine o’clock at night and I really didn’t know what to expect. I just knew that I had to just follow what my coach had always told me and what they’d taught me.”

The nerves were still there, but a turning point came after the semifinal.

“It was pretty nerve-wracking at the time but at one point after the semifinal match I looked at my coach and said, ‘I’m going to the gold match.’ She’s like yeah, to which I replied, ‘I’ve already won.’ At that point it was like a huge weight off my shoulders.”

**![Image 5](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/110926112627-Andre%20Shelby%20celebrating%20on%20winning%20gold%20in%20Rio%202016.jpg)**In the gold medal match, Shelby faced Alberto Simonelli, the same archer who had defeated him at the 2015 World Archery Para Championships.

“It was overwhelming really because even though the weight was lifted off my shoulders going into the match, the year before I shot against Simonelli in a two-arrow shoot-off in Germany for the World Championships. So, I mean it was kind of a redemption at that point because he eliminated me back in 2015.”

In Rio, though, the ending would be different, as [Shelby won 144-143](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y19V1q6VZkw). The gold medal was the culmination of a journey that had begun years earlier and taken him in a very different direction from the one he had originally planned. Shelby had served 18 years in the U.S. Navy and enlisted for another two when a motorbike accident in April 2004 left him paralyzed from the chest down.

Despite the injury and as someone who played football and basketball in high school, Shelby's competitive spirit remained, and so he turned to a variety of sports, including horseback riding, skiing, tennis and water skiing. In 2009, he discovered archery.

Shelby attended a camp led by Jerry Shields, who would go on to represent the United States at the 2012 Paralympic Games in London. He later attended another camp run by Jeff Fabry and Russell Wolfe. Fabry had already won Paralympic bronze in Athens in 2004 and Beijing in 2008 before claiming gold in London in 2012. Wolfe was a teammate of Fabry’s in Beijing and London.

By then, Shelby was hooked, and seven years on from first discovering the sport, he was a Paralympic champion.

**![Image 6](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/110926112648-PARA16_X16_5963.jpg)**For Shelby, the podium ceremony brought the achievement into sharper focus. His thoughts turned to the people who had supported him throughout his career, including his wife, Marilyn, and friends back home.

“The biggest thing was just thinking about my family, my wife, all the stuff she put up with me traveling, all the friends that I had back home, Joe Bailey, Jonathan Myers, Jerry Shields.

“We’d been texting back and forth and calling each other the whole time I was in Rio, and they were saying ‘you deserve to be there. You got it, just shoot the way you normally shoot and you’re going to get it.’ Having them in the back of my mind was just phenomenal.”

Shelby also made history in Rio as the first black Paralympic archer to represent the United States, yet in among all the firsts and fanfare, it was something which took place almost a year later that stands out.

“I think the biggest highlight was when I went back to my hometown (Jeffersonville, Indiana) in 2017 and they actually named August the 7th Andre Shelby Day. I was named Commodore of the Port, which is a huge port for commercial stuff coming in and out. So that really made me think, ‘yeah I’m here.’”

Ten years after Rio, another Paralympic Games is on the horizon, with Los Angeles set to host the 2028 Games. Shelby took a break from competition to deal with surgeries, but the time away has given him a different perspective on his relationship with the sport.

**![Image 7](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/110926112719-Andre%20Shelby%20in%20Jeffersonville.jpg)**“I mean to be honest if I try out for it then I will give it my all and it would really mean something if I did shoot here in the U.S. But I took a little break. I had some issues with surgeries and stuff like that and now I’m realizing the reason I started archery in the first place. It was to have fun and to reminisce with all the people and the athletes I’ve shot with in the past.”

That change in perspective has allowed Shelby to return to the sport with a renewed sense of enjoyment.

“I’ve come back to having fun with it and if I can keep that then if I go out for LA then I think that’ll be a lot better mindset going into it.”

Shelby was in Dublin, Ohio in July for the 2026 Rebel Gear Buckeye Classic where he took gold in compound 50+ men, defeating another adaptive archer, Keith Sekora, in the final. The following month, in the same division, he finished fifth at the USA Archery Target Nationals and fourth in the U.S. Open. He also took fourth at Target Nationals in para compound men.

Whatever comes next competitively, Shelby’s impact on the sport is already being felt away from the field. He now visits clubs and schools to help teach archery, sharing the experience he has gained throughout his career.

“I think the biggest thing is the clubs I go to and some of the schools that I go to and help teach, a lot of people really look to me as a knowledge base or a coach that they can trust you, and I’m willing to provide that wealth of knowledge to anybody that’s willing to learn.”

For the humble Shelby, who turns 60 in December, passing that knowledge on is an important part of his connection to the sport.

**![Image 8](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/110926112939-Andre%20Shelby%20at%20Rio%202016.jpg)**“I’m not the one that’s just gonna hoard it and not do anything but I think the biggest thing is just me helping other people enjoy the sport of archery.”

His gold medal in Rio remains one of the defining moments in USA Archery’s Paralympic history. Since then, Kevin Mather won gold in Tokyo in 2020, while Matt Stutzman and Jason Tabansky both stood atop the podium in Paris in 2024, continuing a run of five U.S. Paralympic archery gold medalists across four Games.

For Shelby, though, the legacy of Rio is not simply the medal. It is the people who helped him get there, the sport that gave him a new direction, and the opportunity to help others discover the same enjoyment he found in archery. A decade after becoming Paralympic champion, Shelby is still finding new ways to give back to the sport that changed his life.

You can watch the [full interview](https://youtu.be/ODmJ-xFCftg) with 2016 Paralympic Games gold medalist, Andre Shelby, as he reflects on his Rio success 10 years on.

# USA Archery News

### September 14, 2026

# Ten years on, Andre Shelby reflects on historic Rio gold and a lasting archery legacy

**![Image 4](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/110926110849-Andre%20Shelby%202016%20podium%20in%20Rio.jpg)Andre Shelby became Paralympic champion at the Rio Games on September 14, 2016. Ten years on, the moment remains difficult for him to fully comprehend.**

“Actually, about a month ago I just looked at all the matches that I shot in Rio and it’s still hard to believe,” Shelby said.

Shelby’s journey to the Paralympic podium had taken him through a long competition day in Rio, beginning around 7 a.m. and continuing until his final match late that evening.

“My last match was like eight, nine o’clock at night and I really didn’t know what to expect. I just knew that I had to just follow what my coach had always told me and what they’d taught me.”

The nerves were still there, but a turning point came after the semifinal.

“It was pretty nerve-wracking at the time but at one point after the semifinal match I looked at my coach and said, ‘I’m going to the gold match.’ She’s like yeah, to which I replied, ‘I’ve already won.’ At that point it was like a huge weight off my shoulders.”

**![Image 5](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/110926112627-Andre%20Shelby%20celebrating%20on%20winning%20gold%20in%20Rio%202016.jpg)**In the gold medal match, Shelby faced Alberto Simonelli, the same archer who had defeated him at the 2015 World Archery Para Championships.

“It was overwhelming really because even though the weight was lifted off my shoulders going into the match, the year before I shot against Simonelli in a two-arrow shoot-off in Germany for the World Championships. So, I mean it was kind of a redemption at that point because he eliminated me back in 2015.”

In Rio, though, the ending would be different, as [Shelby won 144-143](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y19V1q6VZkw). The gold medal was the culmination of a journey that had begun years earlier and taken him in a very different direction from the one he had originally planned. Shelby had served 18 years in the U.S. Navy and enlisted for another two when a motorbike accident in April 2004 left him paralyzed from the chest down.

Despite the injury and as someone who played football and basketball in high school, Shelby's competitive spirit remained, and so he turned to a variety of sports, including horseback riding, skiing, tennis and water skiing. In 2009, he discovered archery.

Shelby attended a camp led by Jerry Shields, who would go on to represent the United States at the 2012 Paralympic Games in London. He later attended another camp run by Jeff Fabry and Russell Wolfe. Fabry had already won Paralympic bronze in Athens in 2004 and Beijing in 2008 before claiming gold in London in 2012. Wolfe was a teammate of Fabry’s in Beijing and London.

By then, Shelby was hooked, and seven years on from first discovering the sport, he was a Paralympic champion.

**![Image 6](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/110926112648-PARA16_X16_5963.jpg)**For Shelby, the podium ceremony brought the achievement into sharper focus. His thoughts turned to the people who had supported him throughout his career, including his wife, Marilyn, and friends back home.

“The biggest thing was just thinking about my family, my wife, all the stuff she put up with me traveling, all the friends that I had back home, Joe Bailey, Jonathan Myers, Jerry Shields.

“We’d been texting back and forth and calling each other the whole time I was in Rio, and they were saying ‘you deserve to be there. You got it, just shoot the way you normally shoot and you’re going to get it.’ Having them in the back of my mind was just phenomenal.”

Shelby also made history in Rio as the first black Paralympic archer to represent the United States, yet in among all the firsts and fanfare, it was something which took place almost a year later that stands out.

“I think the biggest highlight was when I went back to my hometown (Jeffersonville, Indiana) in 2017 and they actually named August the 7th Andre Shelby Day. I was named Commodore of the Port, which is a huge port for commercial stuff coming in and out. So that really made me think, ‘yeah I’m here.’”

Ten years after Rio, another Paralympic Games is on the horizon, with Los Angeles set to host the 2028 Games. Shelby took a break from competition to deal with surgeries, but the time away has given him a different perspective on his relationship with the sport.

**![Image 7](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/110926112719-Andre%20Shelby%20in%20Jeffersonville.jpg)**“I mean to be honest if I try out for it then I will give it my all and it would really mean something if I did shoot here in the U.S. But I took a little break. I had some issues with surgeries and stuff like that and now I’m realizing the reason I started archery in the first place. It was to have fun and to reminisce with all the people and the athletes I’ve shot with in the past.”

That change in perspective has allowed Shelby to return to the sport with a renewed sense of enjoyment.

“I’ve come back to having fun with it and if I can keep that then if I go out for LA then I think that’ll be a lot better mindset going into it.”

Shelby was in Dublin, Ohio in July for the 2026 Rebel Gear Buckeye Classic where he took gold in compound 50+ men, defeating another adaptive archer, Keith Sekora, in the final. The following month, in the same division, he finished fifth at the USA Archery Target Nationals and fourth in the U.S. Open. He also took fourth at Target Nationals in para compound men.

Whatever comes next competitively, Shelby’s impact on the sport is already being felt away from the field. He now visits clubs and schools to help teach archery, sharing the experience he has gained throughout his career.

“I think the biggest thing is the clubs I go to and some of the schools that I go to and help teach, a lot of people really look to me as a knowledge base or a coach that they can trust you, and I’m willing to provide that wealth of knowledge to anybody that’s willing to learn.”

For the humble Shelby, who turns 60 in December, passing that knowledge on is an important part of his connection to the sport.

**![Image 8](https://www.usarchery.org/images/tinymce/110926112939-Andre%20Shelby%20at%20Rio%202016.jpg)**“I’m not the one that’s just gonna hoard it and not do anything but I think the biggest thing is just me helping other people enjoy the sport of archery.”

His gold medal in Rio remains one of the defining moments in USA Archery’s Paralympic history. Since then, Kevin Mather won gold in Tokyo in 2020, while Matt Stutzman and Jason Tabansky both stood atop the podium in Paris in 2024, continuing a run of five U.S. Paralympic archery gold medalists across four Games.

For Shelby, though, the legacy of Rio is not simply the medal. It is the people who helped him get there, the sport that gave him a new direction, and the opportunity to help others discover the same enjoyment he found in archery. A decade after becoming Paralympic champion, Shelby is still finding new ways to give back to the sport that changed his life.

You can watch the [full interview](https://youtu.be/ODmJ-xFCftg) with 2016 Paralympic Games gold medalist, Andre Shelby, as he reflects on his Rio success 10 years on.

## [Hugh D.H. Soar(1926–2022)](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/2022/11/19/hugh-d-h-soar-1926-2022/)

I just got notified that Hugh Soar has died, which was not unexpected as he was closer to being 100 than 90, but still sad. While one could declare that Hugh was a big fish in a small pond, he was the pre-eminent archery historian of the Western Tradition in the world, in my opinion.

He wrote a slew of books on archery history, all written in what I call a charming, somewhat archaic, style. I had the honor of editing his last book, [The Young at Archery](https://www.amazon.com/Young-Archery-Hugh-D-H-Soar/dp/0991332679/ref=sr_1_4?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-4). Other titles included:

[Straight and True: A Select History of the Arrow](https://www.amazon.com/Straight-True-Select-History-Arrow-ebook/dp/B009PQM7F6/ref=sr_1_1?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-1)

[The Crooked Stick: A History of the Longbow](https://www.amazon.com/Crooked-Stick-History-Longbow-ebook/dp/B00492CFXA/ref=sr_1_2?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-2)

[The Romance of Archery: A Social History of the Longbow](https://www.amazon.com/Romance-Archery-Social-History-Longbow/dp/1594160678/ref=sr_1_3?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-3)

[Secrets of the English War Bow](https://www.amazon.com/Secrets-English-War-Hugh-Soar/dp/1594161267/ref=sr_1_7?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-7)

[How to Shoot the Longbow: A Guide from Historical and Applied Sources](https://www.amazon.com/How-Shoot-Longbow-Historical-Applied-ebook/dp/B085J1VQT3/ref=sr_1_8?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-8)

[Of Bowmen and Battles](https://www.amazon.com/Bowmen-Battles-Hugh-David-Hewitt/dp/0951764519/ref=sr_1_1?crid=1B5SB8W79HD8Z&keywords=Of+Bowmen+and+Battles&qid=1668871790&s=books&sprefix=of+bowmen+and+battles%2Cstripbooks%2C92&sr=1-1)

Hugh was sought out for his expertise by television shows and other media, and his collection of more than 240 bows and other artifacts is among the finest in the world.

Hugh was a member of the Mary Rose Trust Committee. The Trust’s primary aims are to preserve, display and spread knowledge about the 16 th century warship, [Mary Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Rose), which sank in the Solent on 19 July 1545 and was salvaged by the Trust in October 1982. The sixteenth century in England was right in Hugh’s wheelhouse, and the ship contained many, many bow staves and bows and arrow shafts, broadheads, etc.

He received a number of honors in his life and he was a member of quite a few historical archery companies, such as the British Longbow Society, the Royal Toxophilite Society, of which he was General Secretary for eleven years, and he founded the Craft Guild of Traditional Bowyers and Fletchers.

He is survived by his wife, Veronica-Mae, whose writings also graced the pages of _Archery Focus_ magazine, and several children and grandchildren.

I am honored to have gotten to work with him.

# [Hugh D.H. Soar(1926–2022)](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/2022/11/19/hugh-d-h-soar-1926-2022/)

I just got notified that Hugh Soar has died, which was not unexpected as he was closer to being 100 than 90, but still sad. While one could declare that Hugh was a big fish in a small pond, he was the pre-eminent archery historian of the Western Tradition in the world, in my opinion.

He wrote a slew of books on archery history, all written in what I call a charming, somewhat archaic, style. I had the honor of editing his last book, [The Young at Archery](https://www.amazon.com/Young-Archery-Hugh-D-H-Soar/dp/0991332679/ref=sr_1_4?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-4). Other titles included:

[Straight and True: A Select History of the Arrow](https://www.amazon.com/Straight-True-Select-History-Arrow-ebook/dp/B009PQM7F6/ref=sr_1_1?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-1)

[The Crooked Stick: A History of the Longbow](https://www.amazon.com/Crooked-Stick-History-Longbow-ebook/dp/B00492CFXA/ref=sr_1_2?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-2)

[The Romance of Archery: A Social History of the Longbow](https://www.amazon.com/Romance-Archery-Social-History-Longbow/dp/1594160678/ref=sr_1_3?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-3)

[Secrets of the English War Bow](https://www.amazon.com/Secrets-English-War-Hugh-Soar/dp/1594161267/ref=sr_1_7?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-7)

[How to Shoot the Longbow: A Guide from Historical and Applied Sources](https://www.amazon.com/How-Shoot-Longbow-Historical-Applied-ebook/dp/B085J1VQT3/ref=sr_1_8?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-8)

[Of Bowmen and Battles](https://www.amazon.com/Bowmen-Battles-Hugh-David-Hewitt/dp/0951764519/ref=sr_1_1?crid=1B5SB8W79HD8Z&keywords=Of+Bowmen+and+Battles&qid=1668871790&s=books&sprefix=of+bowmen+and+battles%2Cstripbooks%2C92&sr=1-1)

Hugh was sought out for his expertise by television shows and other media, and his collection of more than 240 bows and other artifacts is among the finest in the world.

Hugh was a member of the Mary Rose Trust Committee. The Trust’s primary aims are to preserve, display and spread knowledge about the 16 th century warship, [Mary Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Rose), which sank in the Solent on 19 July 1545 and was salvaged by the Trust in October 1982. The sixteenth century in England was right in Hugh’s wheelhouse, and the ship contained many, many bow staves and bows and arrow shafts, broadheads, etc.

He received a number of honors in his life and he was a member of quite a few historical archery companies, such as the British Longbow Society, the Royal Toxophilite Society, of which he was General Secretary for eleven years, and he founded the Craft Guild of Traditional Bowyers and Fletchers.

He is survived by his wife, Veronica-Mae, whose writings also graced the pages of _Archery Focus_ magazine, and several children and grandchildren.

I am honored to have gotten to work with him.

# [Hugh D.H. Soar(1926–2022)](https://archerycoach.wordpress.com/2022/11/19/hugh-d-h-soar-1926-2022/)

I just got notified that Hugh Soar has died, which was not unexpected as he was closer to being 100 than 90, but still sad. While one could declare that Hugh was a big fish in a small pond, he was the pre-eminent archery historian of the Western Tradition in the world, in my opinion.

He wrote a slew of books on archery history, all written in what I call a charming, somewhat archaic, style. I had the honor of editing his last book, [The Young at Archery](https://www.amazon.com/Young-Archery-Hugh-D-H-Soar/dp/0991332679/ref=sr_1_4?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-4). Other titles included:

[Straight and True: A Select History of the Arrow](https://www.amazon.com/Straight-True-Select-History-Arrow-ebook/dp/B009PQM7F6/ref=sr_1_1?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-1)

[The Crooked Stick: A History of the Longbow](https://www.amazon.com/Crooked-Stick-History-Longbow-ebook/dp/B00492CFXA/ref=sr_1_2?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-2)

[The Romance of Archery: A Social History of the Longbow](https://www.amazon.com/Romance-Archery-Social-History-Longbow/dp/1594160678/ref=sr_1_3?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-3)

[Secrets of the English War Bow](https://www.amazon.com/Secrets-English-War-Hugh-Soar/dp/1594161267/ref=sr_1_7?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-7)

[How to Shoot the Longbow: A Guide from Historical and Applied Sources](https://www.amazon.com/How-Shoot-Longbow-Historical-Applied-ebook/dp/B085J1VQT3/ref=sr_1_8?crid=3TFG6TRJQZW0Q&keywords=Hugh+D.H.+Soar&qid=1668870232&s=books&sprefix=hugh+d.h.+soar%2Cstripbooks%2C88&sr=1-8)

[Of Bowmen and Battles](https://www.amazon.com/Bowmen-Battles-Hugh-David-Hewitt/dp/0951764519/ref=sr_1_1?crid=1B5SB8W79HD8Z&keywords=Of+Bowmen+and+Battles&qid=1668871790&s=books&sprefix=of+bowmen+and+battles%2Cstripbooks%2C92&sr=1-1)

Hugh was sought out for his expertise by television shows and other media, and his collection of more than 240 bows and other artifacts is among the finest in the world.

Hugh was a member of the Mary Rose Trust Committee. The Trust’s primary aims are to preserve, display and spread knowledge about the 16 th century warship, [Mary Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Rose), which sank in the Solent on 19 July 1545 and was salvaged by the Trust in October 1982. The sixteenth century in England was right in Hugh’s wheelhouse, and the ship contained many, many bow staves and bows and arrow shafts, broadheads, etc.

He received a number of honors in his life and he was a member of quite a few historical archery companies, such as the British Longbow Society, the Royal Toxophilite Society, of which he was General Secretary for eleven years, and he founded the Craft Guild of Traditional Bowyers and Fletchers.

He is survived by his wife, Veronica-Mae, whose writings also graced the pages of _Archery Focus_ magazine, and several children and grandchildren.

I am honored to have gotten to work with him.

The bow and arrow were invented at least 60,000 to 70,000 years ago and for 99% of that time children learned archery the same way they learned everything else: by doing. At first a child probably played at archery using a found bent stick. Later, they might have been given a purpose–built youth bow (short in length with a weak draw pull) made from basic materials or from a broken adult bow, cut down. Arrows were probably also “hand me downs” and if a child showed enough promise with the bow and arrow, they might be invited to join the hunter’s circle and begin the arduous task of working their way up from the least desirable tasks.More recently, though, children began receiving instruction in the way of the bow. Eminent archery historian Hugh Soar shares his vast knowledge of how youths were taught during this period, both then and now, starting in his native England, expanding to the rest of the U.K, then out to Europe and the U.S., and also including the Middle East, Africa, and the Far East.Archery coaches and archers who have an interest in youth archery or archery history will love this book. It is packed with history and is charming, too. Fully illustrated and highly recommended!Steve Ruis, EditorArchery Focus magazine

The bow and arrow were invented at least 60,000 to 70,000 years ago and for 99% of that time children learned archery the same way they learned everything else: by doing. At first a child probably played at archery using a found bent stick. Later, they might have been given a purpose–built youth bow (short in length with a weak draw pull) made from basic materials or from a broken adult bow, cut down. Arrows were probably also “hand me downs” and if a child showed enough promise with the bow and arrow, they might be invited to join the hunter’s circle and begin the arduous task of working their way up from the least desirable tasks.More recently, though, children began receiving instruction in the way of the bow. Eminent archery historian Hugh Soar shares his vast knowledge of how youths were taught during this period, both then and now, starting in his native England, expanding to the rest of the U.K, then out to Europe and the U.S., and also including the Middle East, Africa, and the Far East.Archery coaches and archers who have an interest in youth archery or archery history will love this book. It is packed with history and is charming, too. Fully illustrated and highly recommended!Steve Ruis, EditorArchery Focus magazine

# From the Beginning - Archery Hall of Fame History ![Image 2](http://www.archeryhalloffame.com/strpzig.gif) _A Little Bit of History_ _The year was 1969, a group of archers were setting around the dinner table at a Professional Archers Association tournament in Michigan. The subject came up about different sports who had halls of fames and one of the tournament officials said," Wouldn't it be something if someday Archery could have a Hall of Fame like other sports have._ _The seed was sown and that was how it all began. At that time is was really just a dream......._ .........but in 1971The Archery Hall of Fame, Inc., became a reality when the then Archery Lane Operators Association President, Joe Rusinek and Professional Archers Association President Dave Staples put their heads together and presented the idea for a Hall to the American Archery Council (AAC). "The thing that struck me when Joe Rusinek and I proposed the idea' said then Hall President Dave Staples, "was that this group of people [within the AAC] had the vision and the sense of history to offer total commitment to an organization that would [promulgate](http://legal-dictionary.thefreedictionary.com/Promulgate)_To officially announce, to publish, to make known to the public; to formally announce a statute or a decision by a court._ every facet of the sport." "We wanted the Hall to be a way of recognizing those people who had moved the sport forward via their contributions, to he a repository of the memorabilia that changed the sport, and [most importantly](http://www.thefreedictionary.com/most+importantly) to be an educational resource for future archers. The early pioneers who got behind Joe Rusinek and supported the formation of the Hall via a sort of "internal committee" included industry standouts like Bob Kelly, [Jim Doughert](http://encyclopedia.thefreedictionary.com/Jim+Dougherty)y, Jim Easton, Earl Hoyt, and George Helwig of the National Archery Association (NAA), Pat Wingfield of the National [Field Archery](http://encyclopedia.thefreedictionary.com/Field+archery)Field archery involves shooting at targets of varying (and often unmarked) distance, often in rough terrain. One goal of field archery is to improve the technique and abilities required for bowhunting in a more realistic outdoor setting, but without introducing the **.....**Association (NFAA), and Dick Lattimer (Bear Archery and later of the [AMO](http://encyclopedia2.thefreedictionary.com/AMO)**AMO** - America's Multimedia Online ). In 1972 the Hall became a part of the AAC. That same year, at Fred Bear's invitation, the Hall held its first induction ceremony at the PAA Nationals in [Grayling, Michigan](http://encyclopedia.thefreedictionary.com/Grayling,+Michigan)Grayling is a city in the U.S. state of Michigan. As of the 2000 census, the city population was 1,952. It is the county seat of Crawford County 6. Grayling takes its name from the Grayling fish that was once prevalent in its lakes and streams. **.....**, and in '76 the Hall incorporated as an independent entity. The Hall would stand alone to protect the integrity of those people who were nominated and inducted. _A Vision for Preserving History_ In the early '70s Joe Rusinek took the lead in creating a vision for the Hall's operation. He served as executive director, and his wife, Jane, assisted him. (The Hall later recognized Joe's leadership with the prestigious Karl E. Palmatier Award of Merit.) Joe, with the able help of Dave Staples and [Don Clark](http://encyclopedia.thefreedictionary.com/Don+Clark)Don, both of whom served as executive directors, Dave basically through the '70s and '80s, and Don from the late '80s until 2004, along with the Hall's Board of Directors, blazed a trail to properly recognize archery's steadfast contributors, while at the same time preserving priceless archery history. A fair procedure for nominating and voting in worthy members was established and with the passing of Joe Rusinek in 1995, Dave Staples, took the helm. "The initial thought process was t o [i](http://medical-dictionary.thefreedictionary.com/induct)[nduct](http://medical-dictionary.thefreedictionary.com/induct)in·duct _v._ To produce an electric current or a magnetic charge by induction. outstanding members of the archery community in the categories of bowhunter, coach, competitor, contributor to the sport, educator, and influence on the sport. That's basically what the Hall's electorate continues to do today. One other category was added, that of Lifetime achievement. The only person to be inducted in that category was Dave Staples after his passing in 2008. Each year official letters of nomination, accompanied by complete biographies and any other supplemental materials telling the nominee's story, are sent to the Hall's office by individual's, wishing to see someone inducted into the hall. and it's up to the Hall's electorate to closely consider these nominations. The Archery Hall of Fame now has approximately 65 electors drawn from the ranks of living inductees, board members, representatives of each national archery organization, representatives of all supporting organizations, and members of the archery/bowhunting media. Soon after Dave Staples took on the Hall's leadership role in the mid 90's , he looked for fresh ideas from Executive Director Don Clark and fellow board member, George Helwig. With renewed vigor the Hall added Dick Lattimer as a member of the board, along with Sherwood Schoch, Maryanne Schumm, and Glenn St. Charles. Dick Lattimer brought a a tremendous sense of history, Maryanne Schumm brought incredible intercollegiate archery and coaching experience, and Glenn St. Charles added the [bowhunting](http://encyclopedia.thefreedictionary.com/Bowhunting)**Bowhunting** is the practice of taking game animals by archery. **Technique** In contrast to a rifle hunter, who may shoot effectively from ranges in excess of 200 yards (about 180 m), archers will usually restrict shots to 45 yards or less, depending on factors such as perspective. _Ready for the Challenge Ahead_ Without a doubt the Archery Hall of Fame has renewed energy and is working hard to set the stage for future efforts to preserve archery history. In the past few years with the passing of some of our board members, new names appear on the board. Rick McKinney, Joe St.Charles, and Billy Staples join M.R. James, Ann Clark, Steve Kaufman, Jane Johnson, Marilyn Bentz and Executive Director, Diane Miller. The big thing is the Hall has found a permanent home with the Bass Pro Shops in Springfield Missouri. and they will house the Hall of Fames memorabilia that will be displayed in our museum for future generations to see. The Hall is doing everything in its power to make sure that it has the archival materials - both artifacts and printed materials - that will allow scholars to intimately know the people and happenings of the archery community/industry. The Hall already possesses a truly impressive collection of materials, including the works and bows of Dr. G.M. Hickman (including a bona fide Geronimo bow), as well as memorabilia from Karl Palmatier, Babe and Henry Bitzenburger, Jean Lee Lombardo, Myrtle "Mimi" Miller, M.R. James and Ann and the late Earl Hoyt, as well as Ann Clark, Jim Dougherty, Glenn St,Charles, Ishi and many other who have been inducted into the Archery Hall of Fame. It's important to recognize the people who made outstanding contributions. Today a lot of people come into the sport without knowing the history, without knowing about the people who came before them!' But the Hall definitely wants [to put an end to](http://www.thefreedictionary.com/To+put+an+end+to) to destroy. - Fuller. See also: End that. The Archery Hall of Fame is keeping its date with history. _Some of the above information is taken from an article written by Jeff Waring, Editor, Bowhuinter Magazine - 2002_
